content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Horizontal and vertical are separate ledgers; only the clock is shared.

content.problem: Ball kicked at 20 m/s at 30°. Find (a) time of flight, (b) max height, (c) range. g = 10 m/s².

steps.reason: vertical component u sin 30° = 10 m/s; T = 2u_y ÷ g. Best: split the motion into two parts and work the vertical one first. Use range formula only if distance is asked.
steps.predictPrompt: Is the horizontal component involved in the flight time?

steps.reason: H = u² sin²θ ÷ 2g
steps.predictPrompt: What vertical speed does the ball have at the very top?

steps.reason: R = u² sin 2θ ÷ g, sin 60° = 0.866
steps.predictPrompt: sin 2θ for θ = 30°: is that sin 30° or sin 60°?

content.question: A gun fires a stone horizontally with a velocity of 25 m/s from a cliff 80 m high. Find (a) the time to hit the ground, (b) the distance from the foot of the cliff where it lands. Take g = 10 m/s².

content.heading: A harder worked example: full triangle at 60°
content.problem: Stone launched at 40 m/s at 60°. Find (a) time of flight, (b) max height, (c) range. sin 60° = 0.866.

steps.operation: Vertical component and time of flight
steps.reason: u_y = 40 × 0.866 = 34.64; T = 2u_y ÷ g. Best: split the motion into pieces, solve the vertical first. If you need height only, use v² = u_y² − 2gH.
steps.predictPrompt: If the launch angle doubled from 30° to 60°, what happens to T?

steps.reason: H = u² sin² θ ÷ 2g = u_y² ÷ 2g
steps.predictPrompt: Which vertical velocity survives the climb — the launch one or the peak one?

steps.reason: R = u² sin 2θ ÷ g, sin 120° = 0.866
steps.predictPrompt: At 30° and 60°, would the ranges match?

content.heading: Go deeper: the projectile in one master sketch
paragraphs: Draw the launch velocity and split it. Horizontal side is a flat line — the projectile's x-axis, unchanged all flight. Vertical side rises, peaks at u_y = 0, and descends. Mirror image on both sides of the peak — the time up equals the time down if the launch and landing levels are the same.

Eliminating t between the two: y = x tan θ − (g ÷ 2u² cos² θ) x². That is the equation of the trajectory — a quadratic; at y = 0 one recovers the range; at the vertex one recovers the maximum height. JAMB rarely demands you recite it but understanding it pays off when 'angle for maximum range' appears.

45 degrees: sin 2θ max at θ = 45°; ranges from any of the 30°/60° pairs come out identical; range at 80° is far shorter — sin 160° = sin 20° small — which is why highlob lobbing rarely wins matches except in desperate situations.
bullets: throw split → flat horizontal line + symmetric arc
y = x tanθ − (g ÷ 2u² cos²θ) x² is the trajectory
45° wins the range; 30° and 60° share it
content.takeaway: The parabola is the same shape whether launched at 45°, 60° or 80°.

content.heading: Go deeper: launches from above the ground
paragraphs: Set the ground as y = 0; the launch point is now at y = h. Vertical equation: h = u_y t − ½gt² with opposite signs for downward launches; solve the quadratic and pick the positive root. For shallow angles the ascending half barely registers, and the whole flight is essentially a delayed fall.

Best mental shortcut: horizontal launch with speed u from height h — fall time t = √(2h/g), independent of u. That independence is a classic JAMB probe: 'a stone dropped and a stone projected horizontally land at the same instant' — both fall the same height, so both arrive together.

For angled launches from a height, drop-height + up-travel stack — the peak comes higher than the launch, and the extra fall distance is (h + H). Applys the same v² = u² − 2as; ranges grow. The sign of u_y makes the only difference from the flat-ground case. If the launch is below the level — a hole or dockside shot — total fall distance is (h − H_if_ascending_finishes_above_zero…) — subtract; don't chase the angle for small h.
bullets: horizontal launch: t = √(2h ÷ g) irrespective of u
from above ground: stack H onto h, then y = h + … → solve
dropped and horizontally projected hit together — same fall h
content.takeaway: Height changes the numbers, never the bookkeeping.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets projectile questions
paragraphs: The archetypes: (1) given u, θ: find T, H or R, or the reverse; (2) 'the same range at 30°' — deduce sin 60°; (3) 'angle for maximum range' — 45°; (4) 'the horizontal and vertical components at impact' — horizontal stays u cos θ; vertical = u sin θ − gT; (5) 'the resultant velocity at impact' — square root of the squares of the two; (6) 'at what instant does the projectile have zero vertical velocity' — t = u sin θ ÷ g, always, no trick.

Rocket flight: powered rocket phase is not projectile motion — thrust dominates; the phase after fuel runs out matches it exactly. Missiles and projectiles: same as the ballistic arc after cutoff. A 'missile fired at 60°' exam stem asks exactly the u, θ, T, H, R block — not thrust calculations; rockets are a story dressing, not a new physics model.

Common wrong answer JAMB plants: 'the horizontal velocity at the highest point is zero.' NO — the projectile never loses horizontal velocity; only the vertical stops. The second plant: 'the acceleration differs between the up phase and the down phase' — no: g is one sign, never reversed. The third plant: 'the speed at impact is less than the speed at launch' — no: at the same level, energy conservation mikes the two speeds identical (neglecting air resistance).
bullets: horizontal at the peak: NOT zero · g: same up and down
impacts at the same level: launch speed = impact speed
rockets: thrust phase — not projectile; fuel out = projectile
content.takeaway: The whole topic is one diagram with three formulas.

lessons.title: Circular Motion
lessons.objective: Use radians, angular velocity and angular acceleration; apply centripetal force F = mv²/r = mω²r; distinguish centripetal from centrifugal force and solve circular-motion problems in strings, satellite orbits and bends.

content.heading: Circular Motion
paragraphs: A car whips round a corner; the passengers lean outward. A long stone on a string loops round overhead. Both are the same mathematics — the mathematics of angular motion, where every second the body turns through an angle rather than stepping forward.

content.heading: Angular displacement and angular speed
paragraphs: Angles in radians: a complete circle is 2π radians. An arc length s subtending at the centre: s = rθ. For circular motion, θ (radians) = angle turned, measured from a reference radius.

Angular velocity ω (omega) is the rate of turning: ω = θ ÷ t. One complete revolution in T seconds ⇒ ω = 2π ÷ T = 2πf. Its unit is the radian per second (rad/s). Angular acceleration α is the rate of change of ω: α = Δω ÷ Δt (rad/s²).
bullets: 1 revolution = 2π rad; rad is dimensionless, label it anyway
ω = θ ÷ t = 2πf = 2π ÷ T (rad/s)
linear and angular link: v = rω, a = rα
content.takeaway: Think in revolutions first; multiply by 2π only in the last line.

check.question: A wheel makes 60 revolutions per minute. Its angular speed in rad/s is
check.why: 60 rev/min = 1 rev/s = 2π rad each second.

content.heading: Centripetal force
paragraphs: Anything in uniform circular motion is accelerating toward the centre — acceleration a = v² ÷ r = ω²r, always pointed inward along the radius. The force supplying it is the centripetal force: F = mv² ÷ r = mω²r.

Friction supplies it on a dry bend; tension on a string rides a stone overhead; gravity keeps a satellite gripped to its orbit. Remove the inward force and the body flies off along a tangent — exactly the way a stone leaves the string when the string snaps.
bullets: F = mv² ÷ r = mω²r — toward the centre, never outward
providers: friction, tension, gravity, spring, magnetic
String snaps ⇒ object departs along a tangent, not radially
content.takeaway: Inward force or the body leaves along a tangent — radius guides its run.

check.question: A 1000 kg car moves at 10 m/s on a level curve of radius 50 m. The centripetal force on it is

content.heading: Centripetal versus centrifugal — and applications
paragraphs: Centripetal force is real: the inward pull. Centrifugal force is the 'outward' pull you feel inside a rotating frame — a pseudo-force that only recipes inside a body sharing that frame's rotation; balance is still provided by the real friction or tension.

Applications: a satellite holds an orbit because gravity acts as its centripetal force; a car slides on a wet bend when friction alone cannot supply the required inward force; washing machine spinners use the small leftover outward way to fling water through holes; centrifuges — blood, milk, air — speed up separation.
JAMB loves magnitude comparison: a heavier body needs a proportionally bigger inward force at the same speed and radius; a longer radius at the same speed needs a smaller inward force.
bullets: centrifugal is the apparent outward force inside rotating frames
all satellites: gravity = centripetal force
F ∝ m, F ∝ v², F ∝ 1/r — measure direction always inward
content.takeaway: Centripetal is the real keeper; centrifugal is the echo inside the spinning car.

check.question: An object in uniform circular motion has a velocity that is directed
options: perpendicular to the radius, along the tangent
check.why: Velocity is along the tangent; it is acceleration and force that point toward the centre.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: JAMB asks for centripetal forces far more than centrifugal ones. Every problem lists ω, v, or T — pick v = 2πr ÷ T first, then F = mv² ÷ r.

content.problem: A 1 × 10²⁴ kg planet orbits a radius 1 × 10¹¹ m at 2 × 10⁴ m/s. Find its centripetal force.

steps.reason: F = mv² ÷ r. Best: use it when speed is printed. If the period is printed instead, the same force is F = mω²r.
steps.predictPrompt: Square the velocity first — which powers dominate the exponent?

steps.reason: powers of ten, before and after squaring
steps.predictPrompt: Does squaring 2 × 10⁴ raise the exponent to 8?

content.question: A 0.5 kg stone moves on a string of length 50 cm at 2 m/s. Find the tension in the string.
hints: Tension supplies the centripetal force: T = mv² ÷ r

content.heading: A harder worked example: a satellite and its orbit
content.problem: A satellite of mass 500 kg moves in a circular orbit of radius 7 × 10⁶ m around the Earth. Its period is 6000 s. Find (a) its orbital speed, (b) the centripetal acceleration.

steps.reason: v = 2πr ÷ T. Best: find the orbital speed first — every later step needs it. If ω is printed, skip and compute a = ω²r.
steps.predictPrompt: Converting the period to hours — do you need to?

steps.reason: a = v² ÷ r
steps.predictPrompt: Do you recognise that number? It is g — why?

content.heading: Go deeper: radians and revolutions
paragraphs: Radians save calculator keystrokes. One full turn is 2π radians; half a turn is π; a right angle is π ÷ 2. A wheel turning at 10 rad/s covers an arc of 10 × r units every second; for a point 0.5 m out, that is 5 m/s at the rim.

Angular acceleration ramps the speed of angular turn: α = Δω ÷ Δt. JAMB pairs α with the statement 'angular velocity is now ω'. Given starting ω, time, and final ω, α follows in one line. Angular displacement also matters: θ = initial ω · t + ½αt² — the rotational cousin of s = ut + ½at².

Connecting rotation to linear motion: every point on the body shares the same ω; the linear speed is greater the further out you sit — v = rω. JAMB loves the question comparing the rim and the hub of the same wheel — different linear v, identical ω at both locations.
bullets: v = rω — same ω for whole wheel, v varies with r
rotational suvat mirror: θ = ω₀t + ½αt²
content.takeaway: Radians are just a rotated ruler — they carry all the same equations.

content.heading: Go deeper: where the inward force comes from
paragraphs: A satellite holds orbit in free fall: gravity points at Earth, but the tangential velocity is so large that the stone continually misses — the orbit is the result of 'falling forever toward Earth yet always missing' — the textbook line for satellites (Newton's mountain thought experiment).

A car on a flat bend relies on friction between tyre and tarmac as its inward provider: F = mv² ÷ r ≤ μN; above that speed the car slides outward — not because of a new force outward, but because friction is simply no longer enough; the car's inertia keeps it straight.

Washing machine spin cycle: the drum acts as a rotating frame — inside it, water gets flung to the drum wall while the drum drills holes allowing it out; your clothes stay in the drum afterwards because the friction between cloth and drum holds them in. Centrifuges separate blood — cells pushed to the end by inertia in the rotating frame.
bullets: gravity = centripetal force in every free-fall orbit
μmg ≥ mv²/r for grip — exceed it and the car slides straight on
centrifuges: rotation sends heavier components outward first
content.takeaway: Centripetal providers are ordinary forces doing an extraordinary job.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets circular-motion questions
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'from n revolutions per minute, find ω in rad/s' — divide by 60, multiply by 2π; (2) 'a satellite orbits in T minutes — find its speed given the radius' — v = 2πr/T; (3) 'the tension on the string' — T = mv²/r; (4) 'the angular acceleration' — gradient of ω–t line or α = Δω/t; (5) 'at what speed does the car skid' — μgr under the square root for v_max.

Trap stems: 'centrifugal force is larger on the equator' — no; the inward providers supply exactly mv²/r; centrifugal is pseudo; JAMB tests the inertia language and the missing-friction idea instead. Another trap: 'the unit of centripetal force is N directed outward' — outward is never an answer; inward is default.

Ordering: radius, period, mass come in any combination; convert hours to seconds, minutes to seconds; never answer in rad/min — JAMB expects rad/s. In satellite problems, the formula cycles turn often: v = 2πr/T then F = mv²/r — two steps both expected; the last wraps up the force.
bullets: f → ω: v = 2πfr — always convert at the first line
outward force is never the answer — centripetal is inward
v_max for grip = √(μgr)
content.takeaway: Circular motion is three formulas in a trench coat — learn three, pass most stems.

lessons.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
lessons.objective: Define simple harmonic motion, identify oscillators, use T = 1/f, T = 2π√(l/g) and T = 2π√(m/k); compute v and a from ω; analyse energy changes; identify forced vibrations and resonance with applications.

content.heading: Simple Harmonic Motion
paragraphs: Watch a pendulum swing; pluck a guitar string; press a tuning fork — all keep time with the same mathematics: simple harmonic motion.

content.heading: What simple harmonic motion is
paragraphs: Simple harmonic motion (SHM) is a motion in which the acceleration is proportional to the displacement from a fixed point and directed toward that point — a = −ω²x.

The fixed point is the mean position. The displacement from it swings between extremes (amplitudes). Every oscillator with equal opportunity on both sides of the mean — pendulum, tuning fork, spring-mass system, plucked string — obeys SHM when one keeps angle small.
Amplitude A is the maximum displacement. Period T is the time of one full back-and-forth; frequency f = 1 ÷ T. JAMB also uses the term 'oscillatory motion' — SHM is its quantitative case.
bullets: definition: a = −ω²x — acceleration → mean, proportional to x
examples: pendulum, tuning fork, spring-mass, vibrating string
A = max displacement; T = seconds per cycle; f = 1 ÷ T
content.takeaway: The minus sign is the whole story — acceleration always pulls back to the mean.

check.question: In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration of the body is directed
check.why: a = −ω²x — the minus sign forces acceleration to point opposite to displacement, i.e., toward the mean position.

content.heading: Period, frequency and the two formulas
paragraphs: f × T = 1; f = 1 ÷ T and T = 1 ÷ f. The angular frequency ω = 2π ÷ T = 2πf. Velocity: v = ω√(A² − x²); maximum v at the mean position: v_max = ωA. Acceleration: a = −ω²x; maximum at extremes: a_max = ω²A.
Pendulum: T = 2π√(l ÷ g). Doubling length quadruples T in squared time — no, doubles √l by √2 times, actually multiplies T by √2. Under small angle only.
Spring: T = 2π√(m ÷ k). Stiffer spring (larger k) ⇒ shorter T; more mass ⇒ longer T. Mass does not affect the pendulum's period at all (small-angle approximation); it does affect the spring's.
bullets: pendulum: T = 2π√(l ÷ g)
spring: T = 2π√(m ÷ k)
content.takeaway: Escape by formula: square root ratios of (l/g) or (m/k) decide T.

check.question: A simple pendulum of length 1 m swings at a place where g = 10 m/s². Its period is about

content.heading: Energy, forced vibrations and resonance
paragraphs: As a body swings through SHM, its total energy stays constant (no friction): T.E. = ½mω²A². Kinetic energy peaks at the mean position; potential energy peaks at the extremes. Both move from one side to the other; sum is fixed.
Equations: K.E. = ½mω²(A² − x²); P.E. = ½mω²x²; total = ½mω²A². JAMB's favourite wording: 'the ratio of KE to PE at general x or given instant' — plug equations and simplify.
Forced vibration: an object driven by an external periodic force, oscillating at the driver’s frequency. Resonance: driving frequency = natural frequency — amplitude peaks to maximum.
bullets: total energy constant; mix of KE and PE at every instant
K.E. max at mean; P.E. max at extremes
resonance: driver frequency = natural frequency ⇒ amplitude peaks
content.takeaway: KE buys amplitude at the mean; PE saves it at the extremes.

check.question: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency
options: is lower than the natural frequency
is higher than the natural frequency
check.why: Energy transfers most efficiently at matching frequencies — the definition of resonance.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: v, a and T questions rarely leave SHM: the three must-know symbols are ω, A, x. Keep the three symbols on your desk from the start of the question.

content.problem: A mass oscillating on a spring has an amplitude of 0.1 m and a period of 0.5 s. Find (a) its frequency, (b) its maximum velocity.

steps.reason: f = 1 ÷ T. Best: read the period first, then flip it for frequency. If ω is asked next, turn it into ω = 2πf.
steps.predictPrompt: What does a 0.5-second period tell you directly about f?

steps.reason: v_max = ωA, where ω = 2πf
steps.predictPrompt: Which speed does the mass hold as it passes the mean position?

content.question: A pendulum of length 2.5 m swings at a place where g = 10 m/s². Find its period.

content.heading: A harder worked example: spring-mass with numbers
content.problem: A spring of stiffness constant 200 N/m carries a 0.5 kg mass set into SHM with amplitude 0.05 m. Find (a) the period, (b) the maximum speed of the mass.

steps.reason: T = 2π√(m ÷ k). Best: the spring formula — mass and stiffness give the timing. If it is a pendulum instead, use T = 2π√(l ÷ g).
steps.predictPrompt: Why does the mass (0.5 kg) enter this formula but not the pendulum's?

steps.reason: ω = 2π ÷ T
steps.predictPrompt: How does ω relate to k ÷ m anyway?

steps.reason: v_max = ωA
steps.predictPrompt: At which point in the swing does the mass attain this speed?

content.heading: Go deeper: deriving the pendulum and spring periods
paragraphs: A pendulum of length l displaced by small angle θ swings because of the restoring component mg sin θ ≈ mg θ. Newton's second law along the arc: ml²(θ'' ) = −mgl θ → θ'' = −(g ÷ l) θ. Comparing a = −ω²x gives ω² = g ÷ l, so T = 2π√(l ÷ g). The algebra requires the small-angle trick — sin θ ≈ θ — JAMB never asks you to prove this but knowing it sharpens the formula's meaning.

Check this from the energy side: K.E. + P.E. cancelling out gives total = ½m g × x_height rise = a spiral decay without damping. For a spring: F = −kx, m(a) = −kx with x'' = −(k ÷ m) x, so ω² = k ÷ m, so T = 2π√(m ÷ k).

There is no mass in the pendulum formula — increasing mass raises both inertia and gravitational pull equally; they cancel. JAMB loves exactly this twist: 'what happens to T if mass increases' — no change, provided l, and g, are unchanged.
bullets: small angle: sin θ ≈ θ enables everything
ω² pendulum = g ÷ l; ω² spring = k ÷ m
mass cancels out of the pendulum period — independent
content.takeaway: Periods come from the restoring force constant — not the mass alone.

content.heading: Go deeper: energy through a full swing
paragraphs: At the mean position: x = 0, so P.E. = 0 and v = v_max — K.E. = ½ m ω² A² = the full total energy. At the extreme: v = 0, so K.E. = 0 and P.E. = ½ m ω² A² = total. At general x: K.E. = ½ m ω² (A² − x²), P.E. = ½ m ω² x². The pair sums to ½ m ω² A² at every x — the invariant.

For a spring: total energy = ½ k A². JAMB may mix: 'behold, a spring of stiffness 400 N/m stretched 0.1 m — how much energy stored?' answer into P.E. against the spring: ½ × 400 × 0.01 = 2 J. When set free, the mass moves through with KE peaks 2 J as it crosses the mean.

Real systems decay: friction and drag bleed energy — amplitude falls over time (damping). Underdamped systems oscillate smaller and smaller; critical damping stops the motion in the shortest time — shock absorbers; overdamping drags slowly — doors on museums, brakes to the floor.
bullets: mean: KE max · PE zero · extremes reverse
½ m ω² A² (mass-spring)· ½ k A² (spring energy)
damping: energy loss till stop · critical: fastest · overdamped: slow
content.takeaway: Total energy is the only fixed book in the library — both ledgers dance in step.

content.heading: Go deeper: forced vibrations and resonance
paragraphs: Natural (free) frequency: an object oscillating freely after a single kick at its own rate. Forced frequency: an object driven by external rhythm; the object swings at the driving frequency, not at its own. Every building, bridge, machine and molecule prefers one rate; force it off that rate and it resists; force it at that rate and amplitudes climb dangerously.

Resonance test cases: soldiers route-march on a bridge — the bridge may start swaying at its own natural rate to the boot rhythm; soldiers break step crossing. Radio antenna: the incoming radio wave carries one EM frequency; antenna resonates only at the station's; tunes away the others off — strong reception.

Shadow applications: microwave ovens resonate the water molecule 2.45 GHz — food heats. A singer at a soda-go glass's natural frequency cracks the glass. Drums and piano chords — the string lifting its amplitude when the resonator box matches — acoustics exploits resonance deliberately. Negative roles: machinery hum ramps into fatigue, phone vibration builds at cover frequencies; insurance note counts these.
bullets: free frequency = the object's own; forced = the driver's
matching rates = resonance = max amplitude
examples: bridges, radios, microwaves, glass breaking — soldiers break step
content.takeaway: Forced is a car listening to the road; resonance is the bridge deciding to agree.

lessons.title: The Gravitational Field
lessons.objective: Apply Newton’s law of universal gravitation, find gravitational field and potential, distinguish conservative fields, state variation of g with height and latitude, relate mass and weight, and determine escape velocity.

content.heading: The Gravitational Field
paragraphs: Everything falls toward the Earth — a coin, an apple, a satellite. That quiet, invisible pull is the gravitational field, and it shapes everything from rainfall to rocket launches.

content.heading: Newton’s law of gravitation and g
paragraphs: Every body pulls every other body with a force F = Gm₁m₂ / r². G is the universal constant, 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N·m²/kg²; r is the distance between centres of mass. The force acts along the line joining them and is mutual — Earth pulls us, we pull Earth, equally.

Near the surface the same law reduces to W = mg, where g = 9.8 m/s² (or 10 in rough problems). g varies with height (g’ = g(1 − 2h/R)) and with latitude — Earth is not a perfect sphere, it bulges at the equator, so g is slightly smaller there.
bullets: F = Gm₁m₂ ÷ r² — attractive along the line joining centres
g = GM ÷ R² — the strength of the field at a point
smaller at poles > smaller at the equator; smaller with height
content.takeaway: G anchors the universe; g is G in our neighbourhood.

check.question: If the distance between two bodies is doubled, the gravitational force between them becomes
check.why: F is inversely proportional to the square of the distance — doubling r quarters F.

content.heading: Field, potential and conservative fields
paragraphs: A field is a region where a force acts without contact. The gravitational field strength at a point is the gravitational force per unit mass — g itself. Potential (Φ) at a point is the gravitational potential energy per unit mass; V = −GM/r relative to infinity (zero), always negative.

A conservative field is one where the work done between two points does not depend on the path — gravity and electrostatics are conservative; friction and drag are not. Conservative fields pair with potential energy — falling releases it, climbing stores it.
bullets: g = force per unit mass (N/kg = m/s²)
Φ = potential energy per unit mass; always negative; ∞ is zero reference
Conservative: gravity, electrostatic — friction: non-conservative
content.takeaway: Field tells the push; potential tells the debt.

check.question: Which of these is a conservative field?
check.why: Gravity is conservative — energy gained by falling is path-independent; friction and drag are not.

content.heading: Weight, escape velocity and orbits
paragraphs: Mass (scalar, kg) is constant; weight W = mg is a vector, newtons, varies with g. A 60 kg person weighs 600 N on Earth.
Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to break free of a planet’s gravity: v = √(2GM/R). For Earth ≈ 11.2 km/s. Below it, a thrown object returns; at it, the object drifts away forever.

Parking orbit (geostationary) circles at ~36,000 km above the equator with 24-hour period — to TV dishes it looks parked. Weightlessness is not absent gravity — it is free fall: both the space station and the astronaut fall together, so the astronaut floats.
bullets: weight mg — vector, varies with g. mass — scalar, constant
escape velocity √(2GM/R) — for Earth ≈ 11.2 km/s
parking orbit = geostationary; weightlessness = mutual free fall
content.takeaway: Gravity never switches off for the station — you float because you fall too.

check.question: The escape velocity from Earth is about
check.why: v = √(2GM/R) for Earth ≈ 11.2 km/s.

content.title: Exam tip

steps.predictPrompt: What is the value of r² for r = 2 m?

steps.predictPrompt: Is 6.67 × 3 = 20.01 or 6.67 × 12 = 80? Watch the numbers

content.heading: Go deeper: G and g — neighbours, not twins
paragraphs: G is universal — it works on every body everywhere; g is private to each planet — Earth's surface g ≈ 9.8 N/kg; the Moon's ≈ 1.6; Jupiter's ≈ 24.8. The book where they belong together is Newton's law: F = Gm₁m₂/r². Set m₂ = mass of Earth at r = R and you get W = mg with g = GM/R² — gravity testing your ability to relate the two constants in one step.

Use g for surface weight questions, G for planet-scale questions: 'mass of the planet' asks for GM; 'weight of an astronaut' asks for m × g. JAMB rarely crosses the wires at once; knowing which is G and which is g saves half the marks.

Mass vs weight on different planets: mass is constant, weight changes — the moon-scale in the pharmacy measures weight, not mass (a coil spring stretches under pull); a balance scale compares two objects against a standard mass — mechanical, unaffected by g. JAMB loves 'weighing machine reads zero' for freely falling frames.
bullets: G ≈ 6.67×10⁻¹¹ everywhere; g ≈ 9.8 at Earth's surface
g = GM ÷ R² — links the two
balance = mass (comparison); spring = weight (stretch)
content.takeaway: g answers 'the pull on me'; G answers 'the pull between us'.

content.heading: Go deeper: gravitational field and potential
paragraphs: Field strength g at a point = the force on unit mass placed there: g = GM ÷ r². Field lines diverge outward — radial. Potential at that point Φ = −GM ÷ r: the work done per unit mass bringing a body from infinity to the point, and it is always negative because infinity is zero and bringing the body downhill releases energy.

Potential energy difference between two heights near Earth is ΔPE = mgh only for small height changes; the full account is ΔPE = −GM(1/r₂ − 1/r₁). JAMB's stem will rarely detail beyond the small-h limit — use mgh for ordinary launches and keep Φ in mind for satellite topics.

Conservative field test: repositioning a body anywhere brings the same energy debt; friction and drag do not — how long you walked does matter at your legs. In a conservative gravitational field, total energy is conserved between any two points; work done by gravity = −ΔPE.
bullets: field g = GM ÷ r² (radial lines outward)
Φ = −GM/r — negative at finite r, zero at infinity
ΔPE near Earth = mgh; in orbit use −GM(1/r₂ − 1/r₁)
content.takeaway: g is push/unit mass; Φ is winter of where energy goes.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets gravitation questions
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'force between two masses' — direct F = Gm₁m₂/r², often in powers of ten; (2) 'if r doubles, F becomes' — inverse square; (3) 'a planet with different g' — weight scales linearly with g, mass constant; (4) 'escape velocity' — no trick, two substitutions into √(2GM/R); (5) 'an object weighs X at surface and Y at height' — g falls off with r; (6) 'parking orbit' — equator-aligned, 24 h; (7) 'why do astronauts float' — mutual free fall.

Value of g itself appears: 'at the surface of a planet of mass M and radius R' — write g = GM/R² and plug; or find 'the mass of the planet given surface g and R'. Cross-planet ratios: g ∝ M/R² dominates — doubling mass multiplies g by two; doubling radius quarters it.

Trap stems: 'the astronaut in ISS orbits at 400 km — his/her weight is zero' — no: roughly 90% of surface g acts there; he has mass, she has inertia; it is apparent weightlessness. Reading too much into 'parking orbit' — means geostationary (24-hour) AND orbiting above the equator — the satellite appears parked; they are technically 'fixed' to one longitude.
bullets: inverse square: doubling r quarters F
g at surface: GM/R² — two unknowns often given at once
weightlessness = mutual free fall — never 'no gravity'
content.takeaway: Two constants, mixed slides, every question — draw the planet chain.

lessons.title: Equilibrium of Coplanar Forces
lessons.objective: Apply the conditions for equilibrium of coplanar forces, use triangle and polygon laws, Lami’s theorem and resolution of forces into perpendicular components; find resultant and equilibrant; apply to roadside and building problems.

content.heading: Equilibrium of Coplanar Forces
paragraphs: Three ropes tie a market stall together; the stall sits still. Four pulls in four directions — yet nothing moves. Physicists call this equilibrium: forces are real but balance to nothing and no motion replaces rest.

content.heading: The conditions for equilibrium
paragraphs: For coplanar forces — all lying in one plane — a body stays at rest (or at constant speed) when (1) the vector sum of forces is zero, or (2) the resolution in two perpendicular directions is zero in both directions: ΣFₓ = 0 and ΣF_y = 0.

For two or more forces: if they act in line, add with signs; at angle, resolve into components; the polygon-of-forces closed figure test says resultant = 0 when the forces drawn tip-to-tail form a closed loop.
Equilibrant is the single force that exactly balances a resultant — equal magnitude, opposite direction.
bullets: ΣFₓ = 0 AND ΣF_y = 0 — both components zero
or ΣF vector = 0 — one rule in all shapes
closed polygon ⟺ resultant is zero
content.takeaway: If all forces cancel out, the restful body has earned its rest.

check.question: Three coplanar forces keep a body in equilibrium. Which is the necessary condition?
options: sum of forces is equal to the weight
check.why: Equilibrium requires zero net force in both perpendicular directions.

content.heading: Triangle law and polygon law
paragraphs: Triangle law: if two forces acting at a point are represented by two sides of a triangle in order, the third side taken in reverse represents their resultant in magnitude and direction.

Polygon law: extends the triangle law to any number of coplanar forces — draw all forces tip-to-tail, join the open ends; the closing side is the resultant. A closed polygon means zero resultant — the equilibrium case.
These are graphical methods — a scale drawing honest enough for JAMB; construct with protractor and ruler, check the closing side against the table.
bullets: two forces → triangle; close the triangle, the third side is R
many forces → polygon; open ends joined give the resultant
closed polygon = equilibrium, no movement
content.takeaway: Arrows closed in a loop spell 'rest'; arrows open spell 'motion'.

check.question: The resultant of two forces represented by two sides of a triangle is given by the
check.why: The triangle is drawn in order — the third side, reversed, closes it in the resultant's direction.

content.heading: Lami’s theorem and resolution of forces
paragraphs: Lami’s theorem: if three coplanar forces keep a body in equilibrium, each force is proportional to the sine of the angle opposite it: F₁/sin α = F₂/sin β = F₃/sin γ. Use it when the angles are known but not the magnitudes.
Resolution: every force has two perpendicular components: Fcosθ along the axis, Fsinθ across it. Add the components on each axis, then check: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0.
Resultant: after resolving, the net pair (X, Y) rebuilds R = √(X² + Y²). Equilibrant: the single force opposite the resultant in direction and equal in magnitude.
bullets: Lami: F₁/sin α = F₂/sin β = F₃/sin γ
resolve into perpendicular components first
resultant √(Fx² + Fy²); equilibrant = same size, opposite sense
content.takeaway: Lami for when the angles shout and the sizes whisper.

check.question: Three coplanar forces keep a body in equilibrium. The ratio of a force to the sine of its opposite angle is
options: the same for all three forces
check.why: Lami’s theorem: the three ratios are identical.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Draw the force diagram before any formula. Almost every equilibrium stem asks for tension or compression — one line, always with an angle.

content.problem: Forces 50 N and 30 N at 60°. Find (a) resultant, (b) its angle from the 50 N force.

steps.reason: ΣFₓ and ΣF_y on the chosen axes. Best: add the parts on each axis, then Pythagoras when the legs are right angles. If components feel messy, use the parallelogram law.
steps.predictPrompt: What is cos 60°?

steps.reason: R = √(X² + Y²)
steps.predictPrompt: Compute 65² + 26² — does the answer pass 70 easily?

steps.reason: tan θ = Y ÷ X
steps.predictPrompt: If the 30 N force were doubled, the angle would — grow or shrink?

hints: weight = 50 N; two tensions+wall reaction oppose it
angles opposite each force are needed — draw the triangle

content.problem: Three coplanar forces 6 N, 8 N, 10 N in equilibrium. Find the angle opposite 6 N.

steps.operation: Identify the sides of a force triangle
steps.reason: the three forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle. Best: Lami’s theorem for three concurrent forces. If that feels awkward, resolve on two axes.
steps.predictPrompt: Which is the longest side — the 10 N force?

steps.reason: F₁/sin α = constant for a stable equilibrium
steps.result: angle opposite 6 N: sin α = 6/k; angle opposite 8 N: sin β = 8/k; angle opposite 10 N: sin γ = 10/k
steps.predictPrompt: What is k? Adding all three angles reaches 360°.

steps.predictPrompt: α + β + 90° = 180° for a closed triangle — does 36.9 + 53.1 + 90 = 180?

content.heading: Go deeper: resolving forces in two directions
paragraphs: Forces act in one plane; split them into horizontal and vertical components. A force of 50 N at 30° above horizontal: X = 50 cos 30° ≈ 43.3 N eastward, Y = 50 sin 30° = 25 N upward. The net force is a single pair (43.3 east, 25 up) and any problem reduces to those two components.

When several forces act, add the Xs among themselves and the Ys among themselves; equilibrium holds when both sets cancel: ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0. A boy pulling a cart north while the wind pushes east is steady when his pull's forward part and the wind's backward drag cancel on both axes separately.

Components can fail when the angle is wrong: selecting sin instead of cos. The fastest check is physical: the bigger component is always opposite the shallower angle — cos of the shallower angle gives the bigger part.
bullets: X = F cos θ · Y = F sin θ
ΣFx = 0 for horizontal balance; ΣFy = 0 for vertical balance
sin θ pairs with its θ; cos θ pairs with its plane — stay consistent
content.takeaway: Two opposing axes are easier than three opposing angles.

content.heading: Go deeper: Lami’s theorem from the quiet inside
paragraphs: Three forces in equilibrium form a closed triangle. Each side represents one force; each interior angle opposes its own force — draw the triangle with the forces tip-to-tail and everything you want sits on the page.

The mathematics behind Lami is just the sine rule applied to the force triangle: F₁ ÷ sin α, F₂ ÷ sin β, F₃ ÷ sin γ are equal constants. For the 6-8-10 case above, the constants are 10 (opposite the 90° angle) and 6-8 give 0.6-0.8 — matches arcsin values.

When Lami's theorem is too slow, fall back on X/Y: resolution always works; labelling the correct angle every time is where it breaks. Pipeline for examinations: draw the force triangle → compute angles → F₁/sin α = F₂/sin β = F₃/sin γ — any one force equals the others per sine.
bullets: closed tip-to-tail force triangle
F ÷ sin(opposite) is constant
solve sin ratios: F unknown = F_other × sin ratio
content.takeaway: Force triangles are slower on paper but cost zero formula errors.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets equilibrium problems
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'three forces keep a body in equilibrium — find angle or force': Lami ratio or closed triangle; (2) 'the tension in the rope holding a weight' — cos or sin of the angle with the wall; (3) 'a man holds a load with two ropes' — symmetry: each rope bears W ÷ (2 sin θ); (4) 'a lamp hangs from two chains making angles θ and β with the wall, find their tensions' — Lami answer √(T₁/ sin α = T₂/sin β) or resolve on both axes; (5) 'a block resting is pulled by two horizontal forces — find the remaining friction' — ΣFx = 0 tells you where the missing number lives.

Traps: the angle in the problem can be measured from the wall or the vertical — get it consistent before substituting into sin or cos; 'coplanar' all forces in one plane — JAMB rarely leaves the plane; a force pair of equal size at 60° is not the equilibrant of the third — do the sum of all three, not two; 'stable equilibrium' wording belongs to the stability topic — moments — don't answer on dimensions from this section.

'Resultant' vs 'equilibrant': in equilibrium, the resultant of the applied forces is cancelled by a further force — the equilibrant. Equal in size, opposite in sense. JAMB swaps the two keywords on purpose; read which one the question asks for.
bullets: resolve on both axes; ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0
angle from vertical ÷ angle from horizontal — consistently
equilibrant = resultant, other way round
content.takeaway: Every equilibrium question: draw four arrows. Whichever section of the page has three arrows moving, the fourth is visible.

lessons.title: Moments of Forces and Stability
lessons.objective: Apply the principle of moments, find moments and couples, compute torques, applications in levers and machines, locate centres of gravity, and distinguish stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium.

content.heading: Moments of Forces and Stability
paragraphs: A tyre sticks on a spanner. A bodybuilder lifts a weight near his body. That is the moment of a force doing work: the ruler is in on the secret.

content.heading: Moment of a force and the principle of moments
paragraphs: Moment of a force about a point = F × perpendicular distance from the point (newton-metre, N·m); direction: clockwise or anticlockwise.
Principle of moments for equilibrium: clockwise = anticlockwise about any point. A beam balanced: 4 kg at 50 cm left, 10 kg at 20 cm right ⇒ 4 × 50 = 200 balances 10 × 20 = 200.
A couple is two parallel, equal, opposite forces not in the same line; torque = one force × distance; pure rotation, no net force.
bullets: M = F × d — clockwise or anticlockwise
equilibrium: CW moments = ACW moments about any point
couple: zero resultant; torque = F × d
content.takeaway: Small force, big distance — all machines live here.

check.question: A force of 80 N acts 0.5 m from a pivot. The moment is

content.heading: Conditions for equilibrium of rigid bodies
paragraphs: Rigid body: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 AND ΣM = 0 — no net force and no net moment.
A beam supported at two points: take moments about one support — the unknown reaction on that point drops out (moment zero), the other stays in one term.
A couple is two parallel, equal, opposite forces not in the same line; its moment (torque) = one force × distance between them. Couples spin taps, keys and screwdrivers — no net force, pure rotation.
bullets: rigid body: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, AND ΣM = 0
take moments about awkward pivots to eliminate unknown forces
couple = pure rotation, zero net force
content.takeaway: Rigid bodies fail by rotation, not sliding — power belongs to moments.

check.question: Two equal and opposite forces of 20 N act at 0.4 m apart on a wheel. The couple is
check.why: Couple = F × d = 20 × 0.4 = 8 N·m; resultant forces cancel.

content.heading: Centre of gravity and stability
paragraphs: The centre of gravity (CG) is the point through which the body's total weight acts. It matters for balance: hang a body from any point and the CG sits directly below the hang point at rest.
Stable equilibrium: small tilt returns the body upright — CG rises and falls. Unstable: small tilt topples — CG falls. Neutral: CG keeps the same height anywhere along the path.
Stability rises with a lower centre of gravity and a wider base — loaded double-decker buses wobble less than empty ones, race cars hug the ground, and a pencil on its tip falls at a breath.
bullets: CG: total weight acts through it
stable → small push returns; unstable → topples; neutral → stays put
wide base, low CG — the stable trio
content.takeaway: Low CG, wide base — the first law of anything not meant to fall over.

check.question: A book lying flat on a table is in what kind of equilibrium?
check.why: Any small tilt lifts the CG and it settles back — stable equilibrium.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Moments are the bulk of mechanics credits — forces list, arms list, one awkward pivot.

steps.reason: moments eliminate the near support — only R₂ stays
steps.predictPrompt: Why does the beam weight act at 2 m — its centre of gravity?

steps.reason: R₁ = total − R₂
steps.predictPrompt: Does R₁ + R₂ = 500 N settle to 175 + 325?

hints: moments on each side must cancel — take moments about the pivot
left = 0.6 kg·m vs right = 0.8 kg·m — not balanced; add 0.2 kg at 1.0 m on the left side

content.problem: Beam (4 m, 100 kg), two end supports. A 60 kg load sits 1 m from one end. Find each reaction.

steps.reason: both supports hold beam + load. Best: bundled load (R₁ + R₂), then moments about one end. If subtraction feels awkward, write two separate moment equations.
steps.predictPrompt: Which side carries more, the near load or the far?
