content.heading: Go deeper: the levers of life
paragraphs: Every machine in motion lives on moments or levers. First-class lever: fulcrum between effort and load — see-saw, scissors, crowbar — can multiply force or distance. Second-class: load between fulcrum and effort — wheelbarrow, nutcracker — multiplies force strongly but moves load in a short range. Third-class: effort between fulcrum and load — tongs, fishing rod, human forearm — never multiplies force, trades force for distance.

Wheel and axle: outer radius R and inner r; M.A. = R ÷ r; e.g., a door knob — small force at big wheel turns through a big torque at the axle. Pulleys: fixed pulley changes direction; movable pulley halves the needed force (M.A. = 2); compound pulleys trade force for cord length per pulley added.

Gear systems — bicycle chainwheel, differential: gear ratio multiplies torque; angular velocity of driver ∝ 1 ÷ ratio. Heavy: wheelbarrows leaned at 45° with load near the wheel — perfect moment arm equals torque management without force friction.
bullets: classed 1/2/3 by fulcrum-load-effort ordering
movable pulley: halves force; fixed changes direction
all machines: force × short distance in → force × long distance out
content.takeaway: Moments make the machine; the correct fulcrum makes the job done.

content.heading: Go deeper: three equilibriums, topplings and centres of gravity
paragraphs: Stable equilibrium — push the body; CG rises then falls to its former level; upright wooden pyramid; cup of tea flat on table. Unstable — push it; CG drops; more tilt follows; pencil on its tip; drum of barrels on a corner; usually instant destruction. Neutral — whatever the push, CG keeps its height; sliding coin; rolling marble; shift anywhere along rails.

Stability rises with a lower CG and wider base: the flat-bottomed double-decker bus bends at corners but never over; a model race car low to the track; a helicopter's skids. A racing tripod narrow and tall topples in a stiff wind — every guy wire out-tops it.

CG location for uneven shapes: divide the object into parts, find each part's CG, weight-weight x coordinates about a reference, coordinate-weight sum ÷ total weight — that x is the CG. Find y the same way. Hang the object twice; the grey area contains the CG.
bullets: stable: small tilt → CG rises → falls back
neutral: CG stays at same height anywhere
unstable: any push releases the CG drop — imminent crash
content.takeaway: Stable objects keep their CG low when invited to fall.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets moment and stability problems
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'moments about a pivot' — identify every force and its perpendicular arm — pitfall: arms measured from the wrong pivot; (2) 'beam reactions at two supports' — take moments about one, other yields; (3) 'centre of gravity of a composite body' — weighted coordinate sums; (4) 'equilibrium type from descriptions' — recognition of the vector trick; (5) 'couple' — direction of rotation, magnitude F×d.

Traps: moments added without direction — adding CW and ACW where signs differ; beam width vanishes from the problem — a 3 m beam supported at both ends with 60 kg in the middle gets 300 N each reaction; forgetting the beam's own weight (uniform beam = moment at its centre); taking moments about the point where the unknown force acts — self-eliminating (moment about acting point = 0).

'Where should the mass be added to bring it to balance?' — no hints; write down everything: total weight × x = CW moment sum, x = Σ(CW moments) ÷ ΣW. Stable/unstable/neutral: y-coordinate of CG rises for stable; falls for unstable; unaffected for neutral. Questions ask to 'state with a reason' — the reason should reference CG height, not aesthetic terms.
bullets: arms are measured perpendicular from the acting force to the pivot
uniform beam: self-weight acts at its midpoint
which type: stable (CG rises) / unstable (drops) / neutral (constant)
content.takeaway: Moments: same direction, same point, Add with direction. That is the end of the list.

lessons.title: Friction
lessons.objective: Differentiate static and dynamic friction, determine limiting coefficient of friction, compare advantages and disadvantages, suggest reduction methods, and analyse viscosity, terminal velocity and Stoke’s law for bodies moving in fluids.

content.heading: Friction
paragraphs: Drag your feet forward on a rough floor; they grip and slide with resistance. That resistance is friction — the silent force at all your tyres, brakes and soles.

content.heading: Static and dynamic friction
paragraphs: Friction opposes relative motion. Static friction: acts on a body at rest when force is applied. Dynamic friction: acts on a body actually sliding. Dynamic is always smaller than the limiting static value.
Limiting friction is the maximum friction just before motion starts: F_lim = μR, where R is the normal reaction and μ (mu) is the coefficient of static friction.
Measuring μ: place the body on a plane, tilt it until it just begins to slide — tan θ = μ. Inclination of textile patches yields the coefficient; pharmaceutical bottles use it the same way.
bullets: static grows with applied force up to a limit; dynamic is constant below it
F_lim = μR — the whole story
tilt test: tan θ = μ at the slip angle
content.takeaway: Static friction wins until the body decides to slide — the slip-limit of motion.

check.question: The coefficient of limiting friction is the ratio of the force of limiting friction to the
check.why: μ = F_lim ÷ R — friction divided by the normal reaction.

content.heading: Advantages, disadvantages and reduction of friction
paragraphs: Without friction: tyres would slip on roads, brakes would fail, books would slide off tables, walking is impossible. Friction enables grip, walking, machines, sandpapering — everything needs a handle. A waxed road at drizzle is a mechanical leak.
The other side: wear and tear (ball bearings die), heat (fires start), energy loss (cars slow on roads), squeaking joints. Every engine sacrifices power to it.
Reduction methods: lubrication with oil/grease, ball bearings, streamlining bodies (aerodynamics), polishing surfaces, using low-friction materials (Teflon on pans).
bullets: Friction is good: walking, braking, sandpaper
friction hurts: wear, heat, wasted power
reduce by oil, bearings, streams, polish, Teflon
content.takeaway: Never eliminate friction — without it your every move would slide into nothing.

check.question: Which of these is NOT a way of reducing friction?
check.why: Roughening a surface increases friction — the others reduce it.

content.heading: Viscosity and terminal velocity
paragraphs: In liquids and gases, viscosity is the internal friction of the fluid — the resistance to a body sliding through it. Unit is poise or Pa·s. Higher temperature ⇒ less viscosity in liquids (warm honey runs thinner); the reverse in gases.
A falling body in a fluid accelerates until the drag equals its weight; beyond that it stops accelerating and moves at constant speed — terminal velocity.
Stokes’ law: drag force on a small sphere F = 6πηrv — η (eta) is viscosity, r is sphere radius, v is terminal velocity. JAMB uses it with oil-drop or raindrop-style scenarios.
bullets: viscosity = internal friction of fluid — decreases with heat
terminal velocity: when drag balances weight, acceleration = 0
Stokes: F = 6πηrv
content.takeaway: Every falling body in fluid eventually stops accelerating — drag always wins time.

check.question: At terminal velocity, the acceleration of the falling body is
check.why: Weight equals drag; net force is zero ⇒ acceleration is zero — constant speed.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: F = μR: normal first, coefficient second, friction third. Beware the angled pull — both arrow and cos enter the chat.

content.problem: A body of mass 5 kg rests on a rough horizontal surface. The coefficient of friction is 0.4. Find the force required to slide the body. (g = 10 m/s²)

steps.reason: on a flat surface the normal equals the body’s weight. Best: F = μN for any flat floor. If an angle is supplied instead, tan θ = μ.
steps.predictPrompt: Is N ever anything other than mg on a flat floor? Try angled.

steps.reason: F_lim = μ × N
steps.predictPrompt: Does the body start moving at 10 N? At 25 N?

content.question: A body of mass 3 kg lies on a horizontal table. A coefficient of limiting friction is 0.5. What force slides the body along the table? (g = 10 m/s²)
hints: F = 15 N — answers a pull less than 15 N; slides only at 15 N

content.heading: A harder worked example: friction on an inclined plane
content.problem: A 10 kg block rests on an incline θ where tan θ = 0.75. The coefficient of friction is 0.3. Find (a) the normal reaction, (b) the force of friction acting on the block.

steps.reason: resolve the force: mg cos θ across the plane, mg sin θ along it. Best: split the force along and across the slope. If only friction is asked, F = μmg cos θ.
steps.predictPrompt: Three-four-five — this is the only triangle you see at 37°.

steps.reason: F = μ × N
steps.predictPrompt: But should F always equal μN? Does sliding happen?

steps.reason: friction can be at most μN — here attempting step asks |mg sin θ|
steps.result: mg sin θ = 10 × 10 × 0.6 = 60 N > 24 N → the block slides; friction stays at 24 N (dynamic, often a little lower)
steps.predictPrompt: Which falls away first — static friction or the applied force?

content.heading: Go deeper: sliding and rolling
paragraphs: Sliding friction is bigger than rolling friction — wheels roll better than roofs skate. Friction also rises with the normal reaction; angled forces change both components; a steeply dragged crate still stays below μN as the horizontal component has reduced normal load; a crate dragged at 37° experiences a less severe verticalnormal effect — N falls by F sin θ, so F pulls while the pass falls faster with less friction force needed.

Walking works because friction acts at your sole backward — ground pushes you forward (reaction) — a friction of at least µR is the only requirement; design of leather soles — Timberland-style ribbed patterns boost µ for light rain.
JAMB lane: 'while driving on a wet road, what happens' — µ drops; braking distances lengthen; lane-keeping gets harder. Skidding is friction taking back its invoice.
bullets: rolling < sliding, lubrication beats all
angled pull: sin drops N, cos provides pull — θ helps both
wet roads: µ drops, braking distance rises
content.takeaway: Angled forces shrink the reaction and the friction — never forget the subtraction.

content.heading: Go deeper: viscosity, terminal velocity, Stokes’ law
paragraphs: Fluids resist shear. Honey flows slower than water — honey has greater viscosity. Measuring viscosity: poiseuille's capillary tube experiments or Stoke's sphere fall — measure fall time, compute η. Unit poise = 10⁻¹ Pa·s. JAMB's oil drop compute: everything is round here.

Falling small sphere under gravity — accelerates until drag matches weight; equation F_net = mg − 6πηrv − upthrust = 0 → v_terminal = (density_sphere − density_fluid) × (4/3 π r³g) ÷ (6πη r) = (2 r² g (ρ_p − ρ_f)) ÷ 9 η. JAMB rarely expects that full derivation; the packet has the answer often.

Raindrops, sand in water, helicopter tumbleweed seeds, blood cells in plasma — all settle in their own terminal velocity. One JAMB stem asks to compare terminal speeds of same radius differing density; answer: ratio = density difference ratio.
bullets: ν decreases with temperature in liquids; increases in gases
terminal velocity: drag = weight — acceleration stops
Stokes: F = 6π η r v
content.takeaway: Viscosity is the fluid's brake; terminal velocity is the trip limit.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets friction questions
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) direct 'F = μR' with horizontal push — plug in; (2) 'force needed just to move the body' — ALWAYS μR; think static; (3) 'a horizontal force P is pulled — if P is above µN the body slides, tells you acceleration' — (P − F) ÷ m; (4) 'at what angle does a block just slide' — tan θ = μ; (5) 'a mass on an accelerating bus — what force holds it down' — horizontal pseudo, friction acts to balance; (6) 'how much force decelerates a sliding body' — dynamic F = µR — one line.

Trap families: (a) N computed from weight without cos (incline); (b) Stokes answer now is expected in mg and v terminal, both small numbers — decimal mistakes abound; (c) 'viscosity increases with temperature' — for gases yes, for liquids NO — tape a magnet to thefridge to remember; (d) 'terminal velocity is low for dense spheres' — exactly the reverse; (e) 'friction increases with surface area' — not in JAMB range; force µ·N does not contain area — memorise it if they ever trick it.

'Coefficient of kinetic friction equals / less than' — less; 'why brakes overheat' — heat from friction = μRN per second; 'rate of heat please' — P = fv — JUB asks for heats produced with power — chips to energy (next lesson).
bullets: μR formula — normal force first, µ second
static ≠ dynamic; μ_static > μ_kinetic always
on incline: N = mg cos θ — never forget the cos
content.takeaway: Friction is simply µ times the normal force — every nuance is a cosine away.

lessons.title: Work, Energy and Power
lessons.objective: Define work, energy and power; compare forms of energy; apply conservation and transformation; interpret area under a force–distance curve; solve numerical problems.

content.heading: Work, Energy and Power
paragraphs: Push a concrete block along a rough floor; every sweated metre is work. Fill the lorry with petrol; every drop is their stored energy; how fast both happen is power. Three quantities, one economy.

content.heading: Work, energy and power defined
paragraphs: Work is force times displacement in the direction of the force: W = Fs cos θ. Units: joule (J). No motion, no work, however hard you push against a wall — the wall does not receive work.

Energy is the capacity to do work. Kinetic energy (E_k = ½mv²), potential energy (E_p = mgh), heat, light, sound, chemical, nuclear, electrical, elastic — all are the same currency in different denominations.
Power is the rate of doing work: P = W ÷ t. Unit: watt (W) = 1 J/s. Kilowatt (kW) = 1000 W; horsepower ≈ 746 W. Electric bills read kilowatt-hours: 1 kWh ≈ 3.6 MJ.
bullets: W = Fs cos θ
Energy = how much work is doable; J or kWh
P = W ÷ t — watts; kW for 1,000 W; kWh = energy, J × 3.6 × 10⁶?
content.takeaway: Work is the bill paid, energy the wallet contents, power the speed of paying.

check.question: A force of 20 N pushes a crate 5 m along the floor. The work done is

content.heading: Forms of energy and conservation
paragraphs: Energy flows between forms but never disappears: Total energy in the universe stays constant — law of conservation of energy. It only changes from useful to less useful forms, often as heat.
Examples: dropping stone — E_p → E_k; hydroelectric dam — water's E_p drives turbines → E_k → electrical energy; bulb — electrical → light + heat; petrol engine — chemical → E_k + heat + sound.
Elastic band: stretched — E_p elastic; fired — E_k. Battery: chemical changes first to electrical, then heat and light.
bullets: total energy constant — it only swaps forms
gravitational E_p → E_k → thermal — the usual route downhill
byproduct: heat is never ‘lost’, only scattered
content.takeaway: Energy never vanishes — it may be useful or it may be warm; the ledger balances.

check.question: When a stone falls freely, the energy that changes most directly is
check.why: Gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy as the speed grows.

content.heading: Force–distance area and numerical problems
paragraphs: The area under a force–distance curve gives the work done by that force. Constant force: rectangle — F × s. Triangular variation: ½ × base × height. Trapezium: ½ (a + b) × h. Once the area is computed, work is computed.
Numerical problems follow one chain: read the problem → draw it → identify F and s (or the graph) → pick the formula. Kinetic energy problems: first get v, then ½mv².
Typical stems: 'area under force–distance graph', 'energy change of a body of mass m dropped through h', 'the work done against friction', 'a 100 kW engine does it in 20 s' → W = P × t.
bullets: area under F–d graph = work
kWh = kW × h; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
route: visualise; find F and s; plug
content.takeaway: Every F–d graph is secretly a workbook in disguise.

check.question: The area under a force–extension graph gives the
check.why: Area between the curve and distance axis is the work done during extension.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Distance or speed plotted against force — the answer is always area. Work units: joules = N × m.

content.problem: A 2000 N car is pushed along 30 m with 500 N. Find the work done.

steps.reason: force directly along the motion, so cos 0° = 1. Best: W = Fs cos θ — always carries the angle. If no angle is printed, it reduces to Fs.
steps.predictPrompt: Is 5000 N at an angle, or you pushing straight forward?

steps.reason: W = Fs cos θ
steps.predictPrompt: Does the weight enter this calculation at all?

content.question: A crane lifts a 500 kg mass to a height of 20 m in 25 s. Find (a) the work done, (b) the power used. Take g = 10 m/s².

content.heading: A harder worked example: energy transformation
content.problem: A 1 kg stone thrown upward at 20 m/s. Find (a) launch KE, (b) top PE, (c) landing KE. g = 10 m/s².

steps.reason: KE = ½mv². Best: use this with mass and speed — height never enters. If height is the variable instead, mgh is your formula.
steps.predictPrompt: What does 'just before it lands' suggest — the same level or lower?

steps.reason: at the top all KE has become PE (no losses)
steps.result: PE = 200 J; also PE = mgh where h = u²/2g = 20 m → mgh = 1 × 10 × 20 = 200 J ✓
steps.predictPrompt: Does the answer pass the same both ways?

steps.reason: total energy conserved; back at the same level
steps.result: KE = 200 J — same as launch (neglecting air resistance)
steps.predictPrompt: Is the speed the same on the way down?

content.heading: Go deeper: energy conversions you meet daily
paragraphs: Charging phone: electrical → chemical (battery). Cooking: chemical (gas or kerosene) → thermal. Typing: muscular chemical → small heat + kinetic finger motion. Falling object: gravitational potential → kinetic → sound + heat at impact.

Electric fan: electrical → kinetic energy of blades → air motion + a small bit of heat at the motor. Electric car: electrical energy stored in battery packs → motor kinetic energy → wheel rotation → motion.

Energy exchange puzzles: 'the energy used' is tracked in two steps — total input × efficiency = useful output. 50% efficient bulb: half of what a 60 W bulb draws is heat; only 30 W of light. Kilowatt-hour cost: charge × kWh — multiply number by rate. Break that chain and you have JAMB marks on word problems involving electricity tariffs.
bullets: charge phoned: electric → chemical
engines: chemical → kinetic + heat
deceleration: kinetic → heat and sound
content.takeaway: Every machine is an exchange bureau — energy in, energy out, nothing invented, nothing lost.

content.heading: Go deeper: the force–distance graph
paragraphs: A constant force on paper: imagine a truck pushing a car 10 m on the floor; the graph is a flat line at F for 10 m; the rectangular area equals F × 10 = work done. It pays to notice small numbers: 2 N × 10 m = 20 J.

A ramp of force on paper: another machine increases force gradually from zero to F over a distance; the graph is a triangle; area = ½ F × d; work = half the rectangle. Many JAMB F-d problems are exactly this shape.
Trapezium: force falls from 8 N to 2 N linearly over 5 m — area = ½ (8 + 2) × 5 = 25 J. Calculating work from a piecewise-linear graph is always area-vs.-formula; a calculator drum-roll handles both.
bullets: rectangle: F × d
triangle: ½ × F × d
trapezium: ½ (a + b) × h — really just two triangles stacked
content.takeaway: Under a force curve, sweep and count — area is work.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets work and power problems
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'work done by a force through a distance' — W = Fs cos θ; (2) 'power of a machine that does W in t' — P = W/t; (3) 'cost of electrical energy' — kWh × tariff; (4) 'a force applied at angle θ' — cos θ enters; (5) 'stretched spring work' — ½ k x² or read the area under F–x graph; (6) 'energy transformation' — identify before and after forms; (7) 'area under F–d graph' — composite area only.

Truck vs car question: 'a force of 5000 N is required to move a vehicle at a constant speed of 20 m/s — find the power exerted' — this is P = Fv, not just P = W/t. JAMB loves to wrap the same physics in algebra slightly rearranged.

Missteps: cosine angle ignored in W = Fs cos θ; W omitted when pushing a wall (no distance); $kWh confused with W; inconsistent units — convert mm to m and minutes to seconds before touching the formula. Separately, the sentence 'a crane lifts a 500 kg load through 20 m in 25 s' silently requires you to multiply weight first — mass has no power; weight does.
bullets: P = Fv — the fast rewrite of P = W ÷ t
θ matters — W = Fs cosθ
life cycle of the paper question: F → W → P, each one feeds the next
content.takeaway: Energy chain in exam order: find F, then W, then P — nothing else matters until all three flow.

lessons.title: Energy and the Needs of Society
lessons.objective: Itemise sources of energy; distinguish renewable and non-renewable; identify energy conversion devices, dams, energy and development, environmental impacts, diversification and safe use.

content.heading: Energy and the Needs of Society
paragraphs: No fuel, no light in the hallway; no light, no hospital at night; no energy, no laptop, no machine at the market, no bus from Ibadan. Energy is how a country moves, feeds itself, cares for the sick, and grows.

content.heading: Sources of energy
paragraphs: Primary sources: those not derived from another (coal, crude oil, sun, wind, water, nuclear). Secondary: those derived (petrol from crude, electricity from falling water).

Renewable energy — sunlight, wind, water (hydro), biomass, geothermal — replenishes naturally. Non-renewable — coal, crude oil, natural gas, nuclear fuels — are finite; Nigeria has oil and gas but volatile prices, import dependence, imported fuel exchange costs.
Nigeria's giants: Kainji, Jebba and Shiroro dams supply hydroelectric power; gas thermal plants feed Lagos; solar mini-grids in Sokoto, Kaduna and savannah settlements reach off-grid communities.
bullets: primary: not derived from another; secondary: derived
renewable: sun, wind, hydro, biomass, geothermal
non-renewable: coal, oil, gas, uranium
content.takeaway: Every light bulb is a decision about which source it drinks from.

check.question: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
check.why: Sunlight is endlessly supplied; coal, oil and gas are finite.

content.heading: Energy uses and energy conversion
paragraphs: Homes: cooking, lighting, entertainment, refrigeration. Work: factories, clinics, schools, shops, farms. Transport: vehicles run on petrol (chemical to mechanical), public transport mostly of the same source. Hotels in Lagos run round-the-clock air-conditioning off the grid when it works, and off gensets when it doesn't.

Energy conversions: mechanical → electrical (generator), chemical → thermal (stove), electrical → thermal (heater), solar → electrical (photovoltaic). Every device is an exchange — none makes energy; all move it from one mould to another.
Devices: power stations (dams, thermal gas plants, wind, solar), transformers, diesel generators, NEPA/PH supply, distribution lines, solar panels, biogas plants, kerosene stoves.
bullets: mechanical → electrical: generators
chemical → thermal: stoves
solar → electrical: photovoltaics
content.takeaway: Every appliance in the house is an energy translator.

check.question: The conversion in a hydroelectric dam is
check.why: Falling water drives turbines — gravitational potential energy (stored water) becomes mechanical, then electrical.

content.heading: Energy, society and the environment
paragraphs: Energy powers development: electrified clinics deliver vaccines at night; electrified schools keep children reading after dark; electrified factories create jobs. Nigeria spends billions on diesels while grumbling about fuel prices — the paradox of energy poverty.

Impact of energy use: global warming, greenhouse gas (CO₂ from petrol, coal, gas), air pollution (sulfur, oxides of nitrogen), oil spills (Bodo, Niger Delta, Ogoniland), gas flaring, deforestation from firewood.

Safe use: fuel-efficient cooking stoves, switching off when leaving a room, solar home systems for rural areas, safe disposal of batteries, public education; electricity accidents account for a large fraction of NIIE emergencies.
bullets: energy poverty ruins health, education and jobs
greenhouse gases carry heat from the earth and warm it
switch off, cook efficiently, respect wires
content.takeaway: How a country burns decides whether it thrives or cooks.

check.question: The main environmental effect of petrol use is
check.why: Burning petrol releases CO₂, a greenhouse gas that traps heat.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The exam wants you to argue, not guess: renewable = examples, non-renewable = examples, side effects of petrol = always CO₂ and greenhouse. 'Diversification' is the magic word for mixing sources.

content.problem: A 60 W electric bulb is used for 5 hours a day for 30 days. If electricity costs ₦70 per kWh, find the total bill.

steps.reason: power times hours, then ÷ 1000. Best: convert to kW (0.06 kW), times hours, times tariff. If kWh is not asked, use plain P × t in joules.
steps.predictPrompt: 60 W — does W stay in watts here, or do you divide by 1000 first?

steps.reason: kWh × tariff
steps.predictPrompt: Would the same formula work for a kW's electric kettle used 10 times?

content.question: Give three reasons why Nigeria should diversify its energy sources away from crude oil.
hints: development of renewables for remote communities without the grid

content.heading: A harder worked example: dam energy
content.problem: Water from a dam flows through a turbine at 20 m/s. The turbine generates electrical energy from mechanical energy. What height h must the water fall to get that speed neglecting losses? Take g = 10 m/s².

steps.reason: PE lost equals KE gained; energy is conserved. Best: mgh = ½mv² when nothing escapes. If only height is asked, rearrange v² = 2gh.
steps.predictPrompt: The mass cancels — always?

steps.reason: plug values
steps.predictPrompt: Does a higher turbine get more energy, or the same?

content.heading: Go deeper: dams, solar and nuclear in Nigeria
paragraphs: Hydropower: Kainji, Jebba and Shiroro — the hydro triad, combined ≈ 1.9 GW; output falls in the dry season. Other hydro: Ikere Gorge, Zungeru.

A typical 2 kW rooftop solar array in Lagos yields about 10 kWh on a clear day — enough to run a fridge, fans, a TV and efficient lighting. In the wet season yield can drop below 40% of that, so generators persist as backup. Off-grid cooperatives resell surplus power to neighbours at mini-grid rates.

Nigeria energy crises: unmet demand costs an estimated 2-3% of GDP yearly; about 45 million Nigerians have no electricity at all. Kerosene and diesel still power millions of businesses — rationalising that dependence is the diversification story the exam wants.
Solar: one of the cheapest today; Sokoto, Kaduna and Borno pilot farms feed national grid; prepaid solar meters popular in villages; pv panels 25% efficiency typical.
Nuclear: Nigeria has a research reactor at Zaria (not yet commercial power). Wind: Katsina wind farm. Oil spills: Niger Delta creeks carry the scars.
bullets: Kainji, Jebba, Shiroro — the hydro triad
Sokoto and Kaduna feed the solar grid
Zaria: research reactor, not yet commercial
content.takeaway: Nigeria's grid is a patchwork — dams, gas, imports, and off-grid solutions.

content.heading: Go deeper: energy and the environment
paragraphs: CO₂ from petrol and coal — captured in the atmosphere; heat from the sun cannot escape back; global temperatures rise; sea levels climb; savanna expands; coastal settlements drown.
Gas flaring in the Niger Delta: light, heat, wasted fuel and diseases of the lungs and eyes nearby; Nigeria has committed to end it — commitments slow.

Nigeria owns the largest natural gas reserves in Africa but imports refined petrol — mismatch of resource and value; agriculture (firewood and charcoal) drives deforestation; biomass energy can be cheap but must be harvested renewably.

Efficient cooking stoves cut firewood use by about half, slowing local deforestation — proposed as one of Nigeria's cheapest reforestation measures; replacement trees recycle wind and rainfall further than most concrete plans ever will.
bullets: CO₂ from petrol → greenhouse → global warming
gas flaring: poisoning local health and air
firewood: deforestation driver — recoverable stoves required
content.takeaway: Every megawatt has a receipt.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets energy-society questions
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'renewable vs non-renewable' — examples from list; (2) 'a device' — identify conversion type; (3) 'which is best for a remote village' — answer: off-grid solar; (4) 'environmental impact of petrol' — always CO₂ + greenhouse effect; (5) 'safe energy use' — switch off, kerosene stove away from children, no open flames; (6) 'energy crises' — price volatility + import dependency + transmission losses.
'Diversification' means mixing sources — sun, wind, hydro, gas reserves — to reduce shock exposure. Nigeria has 60% dependence on gas thermal plus dams; solar would diversify 30% via mini-grids.

Recall the three-answer triad in every exam question — renewable examples, petrol's environmental side-effects (CO₂ → greenhouse warming), and the magic word 'diversification'. Recite all three, every time.

Nigeria generates barely 40% of its installed ~12 GW at any moment; maintenance, gas supply hitches and transmission losses bleed the rest — that is the exam's whole Nigerian energy diagnosis in one line.

Nigeria questions: 'three renewable sources in Nigeria' — sun, water, wind (Katsina); 'three non-renewables used in Nigeria' — crude oil, natural gas, coal (Enugu coal historically); 'a dam in Nigeria' — Kainji, Jebba or Shiroro; 'a nuclear facility' — the research reactor at Zaria. The exam expects you to know these.
bullets: renewable in Nigeria: sun, water, wind
non-renewable: crude oil, gas, coal
diversify — or suffer single-source shock
content.takeaway: Exam answer bnbbb: name, explain, example.

lessons.title: Photoelectric Effect and Photovoltaic Cells
lessons.objective: State photoelectric emission, write Einstein’s equation hf = W + ½mv²_max, define threshold frequency, work function and Planck’s constant; explain photovoltaic cells and solar collectors.

content.heading: Photoelectric Effect and Photovoltaic Cells
paragraphs: Shine UV light on zinc and electrons sail off its surface. This short letter — the photoelectric effect — forced physics to accept that light, once a simple wave, carries energy in parcels. Each parcel is a photon.

content.heading: What the photoelectric effect is
paragraphs: Photoemission: light of frequency above threshold ejects electrons from a metal. Failure below the threshold means every photon carries too little energy. Brighter below that threshold changes nothing; brighter above steps up how many electrons fly.

Einstein’s equation: hf = W + ½mv²_max — energy in = work function + kinetic energy max of the escaped electron. h is Planck’s constant (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s), f is the frequency of the light, W is the work function of the metal.
bullets: hf = W + KE max — the photoelectric equation
below threshold frequency — nothing comes out
content.takeaway: Light cares about colour, not just brightness — violet works, red often doesn’t.

check.question: In Einstein’s photoelectric equation hf = W + ½mv², the symbol W stands for the
check.why: W is the minimum energy needed to pull an electron from the metal’s surface.

content.heading: Threshold frequency and work function
paragraphs: Threshold frequency (f₀) is the lowest frequency at which photoemission happens. Work function W = hf₀. Below f₀ for a metal, no electron emerges regardless of intensity — intensity affects how many electrons, not whether. A bright red lamp fired as hard as you like makes no electrons emerge; a faint violet just above threshold does.

Different metals have different W: sodium ~2.3 eV, zinc ~4.3 eV. Photons carry packet sizes e = hf — higher frequency photons dribble the most powerful punch. Once above threshold the photon’s energy splits into escape work plus KE.
bullets: W = hf₀
higher photon frequency → more KE per electron
brightness affects number of photoelectrons, not their KE
content.takeaway: Low-frequency light of the brightest flame cannot knock electrons off — colour rules.

check.question: If the photon energy exceeds the metal’s work function, the excess is
options: lost as heat in the metal
carried off by the photoelectron as kinetic energy
check.why: hf − W = ½mv²_max — the leftover is the escaped electron’s kinetic energy.

content.heading: Photovoltaic cells and solar panels
paragraphs: Photovoltaic cell: semiconductor that converts photon energy directly into electric energy. Used in calculators, satellites, remote traffic lights, rooftop solar. Combined cells form a solar panel.
Solar collector: a box with a black plate, water tubes, glazing; sun heats water directly — used for showers and pool heating.

Photovoltaic vs photoelectric: photovoltaic = DC output, semiconductor p-n junction, current produced even at low illumination; photoelectric wants UV and escape from metal surface — two sides of the same photon. One rooftop array in Lagos can power a whole house without a single moving part.
bullets: photovoltaic cells → DC electricity
solar panels = cells wired together for greater wattage
collectors heat water directly — no electricity
content.takeaway: Every solar roof is a silicon meadow catching photons for lunch.

check.question: Electric current produced in a solar cell is
check.why: A photovoltaic cell delivers DC like a battery.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Master hf = W + KE; 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; substitute f or λ only with c = fλ.

content.problem: A metal with a work function of 2.5 eV is illuminated by ultraviolet light of frequency 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)

steps.reason: the photon’s energy. Best: hf − W = KE — frequency is already printed. If W is printed instead, W = hf₀ from the threshold.
KE = hf − W
steps.predictPrompt: Which unit does the work function speak in here?

steps.result: hf < W — no emission occurs; this trick question has one answer: 0
steps.predictPrompt: What does it mean when the photon is too weak?

content.question: A sodium cathode needs 2.28 eV to release electrons. With what maximum KE do photoelectrons emerge when struck by light of frequency 1 × 10¹⁵ Hz? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)

content.heading: A harder worked example: threshold wavelength
content.problem: A metal has threshold frequency 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find (a) the work function in eV, (b) the maximum KE with incident light of frequency 8 × 10¹⁴ Hz.

steps.reason: W = hf₀. Best: threshold frequency straight into Planck's equation. If W is now in hand, hf = W + KE finishes it.
steps.predictPrompt: Convert J → eV by dividing by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹!

steps.reason: KE = hf − W
steps.predictPrompt: Of the two terms in hf − W, which is the big one — and which is the small one?

content.heading: Go deeper: how photoelectric experiments actually run
paragraphs: First verified by Hertz in 1887 — spark gaps shorted by UV. Hallwachs saw discharge only with high-frequency light. J.J. Thomson clarified charge dependence; Millikan measured h to 0.5% accuracy — the metal work function, the charge of electron, e restores mastery.

Each metal has its own work function — sodium 2.28 eV, caesium lower ~2.1 eV, zinc 4.3 eV. A beam's intensity decides number of electrons, not their energy; that is why the mass light above the threshold work function matters, and the mass light below it does nothing.

Photocurrent vs voltage: with negative potential sufficiently large on the anode, no electrons reach — this 'stopping potential' V₀ × e = KEmax.  JAMB may ask: 'find the stopping potential for given light' — V₀ = KE ÷ e awkward in eV → e cancels (KE in eV equals V₀ in volts).
bullets: stopping potential V₀ (V) = KE_max (eV) — same numerical value
work function per metal: sodium 2.28, zinc 4.3 eV
Hertz → Hallwachs → Thomson → Millikan — the history JAMB recycles
content.takeaway: Every photoelectric stem boils down to one hf number vs one W number.

content.heading: Go deeper: photovoltaics and solar collectors
paragraphs: p-n junction solar cells: silicon doped with phosphorus (n-type, extra electrons) and boron (p-type, shortage — holes). Photons with energy ≥ band-gap (1.1 eV for silicon) driven into more motion. Single cells reach ~25% efficiency; commercial panels commonly 15–20%.

Collectors: black plate absorbs, tubes carry water, glass top traps heat — a greenhouse effect on your roof. Simple, flat, inexpensive — Kenya built one of the world's biggest rooftop collector arrays; Nigeria is growing them in the northern solar belt.
Net energy: sunlight delivers ~1 kW/m² at peak noon. Rooftop photovoltaic arrays of 2–5 kW cover a typical home's load, and net-metering (Nigeria started gradually) lets you sell back.
A village off-grid mini-grid: one 20 kW array feeds 80 homes with LED light, a pump and a clinic; batteries charge all day for the night shift; diesel gensets sleep.
Hospitals, schools and clinics outside grid reach use the same formula daily — solar lantern → phone charge → bank app — the exam's cartography of what 'energy for development' actually means.
Solar lessons stay colourful: UV knocks electrons free; infra-red keeps hand-warmers honest; anything past violet gets the escape energy.
bullets: PV: p-n junction; ≥1.1 eV band-gap for silicon
collectors: black plate + tubes — heats water directly
peak sun ≈ 1 kW/m²
content.takeaway: A solar roof is a photon oven with silicon bread inside.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets photoelectric questions
paragraphs: The archetypes: (1) 'photoelectric equation — what is hf, KE or W' — direct substitution; (2) 'threshold colour' — violet or UV works, red does not; (3) 'stopping potential' — the voltage where emission ceases; convert KEmax to volts; (4) 'work function of a metal in J or eV' — one small conversion, easy to flub; (5) 'photovoltaic cells — what type current' — DC.

Trap: 'below threshold frequency' — nothing emerges. Trap: 'brightness increasing' — nothing happens to emitted electrons' max energy; number grows instead. Trap: 'if frequency doubles' — KE max does not double: it increases by hf, not by factor two.

Photoelectric E = hf − W forces everything in Joules; convert from eV first — the unit kills more JAMBs than any concept disagreement. Keep h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ memorised, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. h × typical frequency = ~10⁻¹⁹ J — JAMB loves this scale and anything else.
bullets: hf − W = KE — everything in Joules
stopping potential trade: KE (eV) ≡ V₀ (V)
red below threshold = silence, regardless of brightness
content.takeaway: Two constants, one subtraction — the three-line exam skill.

lessons.title: Simple Machines
lessons.objective: Identify types of simple machines (lever, pulley, wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw); solve problems involving mechanical advantage, velocity ratio, efficiency.

content.heading: Simple Machines
paragraphs: A knife is a wedge; a bicycle a wheel-and-axle; a winch a pulley; a car ramp an inclined plane; a can-opener a complex of two machines. Wherever the human body cannot reach, machines take over — step across them and you cross the river.

content.heading: Types of machines
paragraphs: Lever: a rigid bar that turns around a fixed point. Three classes — first class: fulcrum between load and effort (scissors, see-saw); second class: load between fulcrum and effort (wheelbarrow, nutcracker); third class: effort between fulcrum and load (tweezers, fishing rod, human arm).
Pulley: wheel + axle + cable. Fixed pulley changes direction of effort; movable pulley halves required force. Multiple pulleys form blocks — Ma = n.
Others: Wheel and axle (door handles, screwdrivers, windlass), inclined plane (ramp), wedge (chisels, knives, axes), screw (jacks, bolts, vices), gear (bikes, cars, clocks).
bullets: levers: 1st class = fulcrum central; 2nd = load central; 3rd = effort central
pulley blocks: one movable doubles force, combine more to double again
wheel and axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw — each for specific jobs
content.takeaway: Simple machines come in six flavours; combined they become almost anything.

check.question: Which class of lever is a wheelbarrow?
check.why: In a wheelbarrow, the load sits between the fulcrum (wheel) and the effort (hands) — second-class lever.

content.heading: Mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency
paragraphs: MA = Load ÷ Effort — how many times the device multiplies your force. VR = distance moved by effort ÷ distance moved by load — Vрыр. Ideal machine (no friction): MA = VR.
Efficiency = (useful work out ÷ total work in) = MA ÷ VR × 100%. Never above 100% — impossible to get back more useful work than you put in. Real machines: 20–90%.
Compound machines: combined advantage MA = MA₁ × MA₂. Pulley + inclined plane systems multiply forces.
bullets: MA = Load ÷ Effort
VR = effort distance ÷ load distance
efficiency = MA ÷ VR × 100% — never above 100
content.takeaway: Force × distance in = force × distance out — energy condensed, never free.

check.question: A machine has MA = 4 and VR = 5. Its efficiency is
check.why: Efficiency = MA ÷ VR × 100 = 4 ÷ 5 × 100 = 80%.

content.heading: Machines in practice
paragraphs: Examples: the car jack multiplies force for lifting a tyre; the screw-jack bridge of a skyscraper bridge uses hundredths of a metre per turn to raise hundreds of tonnes; racquetball paddle — two classes of machines in one.
Distance that force travels is always sacrificed: the more force multiplication, the more stretch the effort has to cover. No free lunch — force × distance remains balanced on the scales of energy.
In pulleys: effort up 3 m for load up 1 m with 2 movable pulleys — MA = 3 or 4. A cam and lever lets workers crank a 10-tonne steel plate with two hands.
bullets: car jack lifts tons by tiny turns — force multiplied by VR
MA × VR = efficiency × 100
more MA, less line-length moved — one trade or the other
content.takeaway: Work-in = work-out; machines just pick the ratchet hands.

check.question: A machine has MA = 5 and VR = 5. Its efficiency is
check.why: Efficiency = 5 ÷ 5 × 100 = 100% — an ideal (frictionless) machine.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: MA first, VR in the second breath, efficiency once you have both. Answers always sit between observed force and ideal devices.

content.problem: A pulley system has a mechanical advantage of 3. To raise a 120 N load through 0.6 m, the effort end is pulled down 1.8 m with 50 N. Find (a) VR, (b) efficiency.

steps.reason: VR = effort distance ÷ load distance. Best: use VR — distances only, friction ignored. If stuck, cash-check MA = Load ÷ Effort.
steps.predictPrompt: Which is the longer distance — the load or the hand?

steps.reason: efficiency = MA ÷ VR × 100
steps.predictPrompt: Is MA = VR a sign of zero losses or terrible friction?

content.question: A wheel and axle has a radius of 0.5 m (wheel) and 0.05 m (axle). What force applied to the wheel will raise a 150 N load?

content.heading: A harder worked example: lifting with a block and tackle
content.problem: A load of 400 N is raised by an effort of 100 N using a pulley system. The rope is pulled 4 m to raise the load 1 m. Find (a) MA, (b) VR, (c) efficiency.

steps.reason: MA = load ÷ effort. Best: MA — loads and efforts printed only. If distances appear, cross-check with VR instead.
steps.predictPrompt: What does MA = 4 mean about the effort required?

steps.reason: VR = effort distance ÷ load distance. Best: use VR — distances only, friction ignored. If stuck, cash-check MA = Load ÷ Effort.
steps.predictPrompt: If VR = 4, does the load rise by 1 m for every 4 m of pull?

steps.reason: MA ÷ VR × 100
steps.predictPrompt: Would you accept that answer, or would you suspect a typo?

content.heading: Go deeper: six simple machines from scratch
paragraphs: Lever: pivot and bar. Distinguishing order: 1st – pivot in middle (scissors, see-saw); 2nd – load in middle (wheelbarrow, bottle opener); 3rd – effort in middle (arm, tongs). Effort arm ≠ load arm classes neatly only for lever (VR = effort arm ÷ load arm).

Inclined plane: one length, one height; VR = length ÷ height; MA = load ÷ effort. The Trade-off: distance costs. A 4 m ramp for a 1 m potion — 4 m of pushing instead of 1 m of heavy lifting, but 1/4 of the force.
Pulley blocks: each supporting strand counts one MA point; MA for n-strand blocks is n; a two-block tackle lifts a carton with half your force — the reason pulleys belong on every workshop ceiling.
Compound leverage stacks — MAs multiply; a block and tackle on a lever arm doubles plus doubles; two simple machines can beat six separate trials of muscle alone.
A JAMB-proof rule: there is no 'simple machine' without a moving piece — they are all levers wearing hats — the exam loves to ask which class, never whether one exists.

Wedge: double inclined plane — axe, knife, splitting logs; Screw: continuous inclined plane around a cylinder — jack, camera tripod bolt, vice. Wheel and axle: crank, windlass, capstan; tape measures and bicycle gear-sets include many.
bullets: simple machines: lever, pulley, wheel/axle, inclined plane, wedge, screw
each multiplies force with distance cost
compound kits mend more than their parts
content.takeaway: Choosing the correct class — the whole machine counts, parts or no parts.

content.heading: Go deeper: mechanical advantage numbers everywhere
paragraphs: Pulley block: an ideal 4-pulley system gives MA = 4 (each movable unit doubles its number). Real efficiency: bearings, rope weight and friction drop it — measure efficiency and see ~70%; enough for a 400 kg load — 100 kg effort.
Ramp formula: h ÷ L — lowly inclined plane saves muscle with longer push-time. New Lagos Island buildings use the same principle in loading goods to the third floor.
Gears comparison: effort on the big gear to crank a small one yields high speed, low force; small input to make big output yields high force low speed (bicycle climbing).
bullets: VR ramp = L ÷ h; MA = load ÷ effort
real-world pulley MA = 3–4, efficiency 70–80%
bike gear ratio: force ÷ speed exchange
content.takeaway: Know the order of wheels and you can run the whole workshop without spares.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets simple-machine questions
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'find MA given load and effort' — load ÷ effort; (2) 'find efficiency given MA and VR' — one division; (3) 'gear system with 1000 teeth driving 250 teeth — find ratio' — 4 : 1, wheel-diameter implies direct ratio; (4) 'a 3 pulley block — find MA or distance pulled' — rope distance is 3× height; (5) 'force = 50 N raises 200 N load — MA?' — 4; (6) 'which class of lever is this image' — 1st/2nd/3rd.

Trap: 'MA and VR are always equal' — only in frictionless machines. Trap: 'VR for a pulley block is equal to number of pulleys' — number of supporting strands, perhaps (three strands double the MA; MA = 2; VR = 2). Trap: efficiency never exceeds 100% — a result >100% means wrong substitution, not a super-machine.

Hybrid trading question: 'a 200 N load requires 50 N effort, and the rope moves 4 m to raise the load 1 m' — combined MA = 4, VR = 4, efficiency = 100% (or honest opposite: 400 N MA, 4 — but you're stopped by the same old 100% bookkeeping).
bullets: MA = load ÷ effort
VR = effort distance ÷ load distance
efficiency = MA ÷ VR × 100 — honest below 100
content.takeaway: A machine: three numbers, one question — the exam stays polite.

lessons.title: Elasticity
lessons.objective: Interpret force–extension curves; apply Hooke’s law and Young’s modulus; use the spring balance to measure force; determine work done per unit volume in springs and elastic strings.

content.heading: Elasticity
paragraphs: Stretch a rubber band: it pulls back. Bounce on a trampoline; the mat returns you. Every elastic system follows one law — stress, strain, and a constant called Young’s modulus.

content.heading: Hooke’s law and Young’s modulus
paragraphs: Hooke’s law: up to the elastic limit, extension is proportional to load: F = kx, where k is the spring constant (stiffness), x the extension.
Young’s modulus (Y) measures how stiff a material is: Y = stress ÷ strain = (F/A) ÷ (x/L). Unit: N/m² or Pa. Steel ~2 × 10¹¹ Pa; rubber ~10⁷; copper ~10¹¹.

If a force-extension graph is a straight line through the origin, Hooke holds; its gradient equals the spring constant k. Beyond the elastic limit, the material deforms plastically and never recovers.
bullets: F = kx — Hooke’s law
gradient of force-extension graph = k
content.takeaway: Hooke holds until the strain exceeds the spring’s limits — then permanence follows.

check.question: Hooke’s law states that the extension of an elastic body is
check.why: F = kx — in the elastic range, extension and force are proportional.

content.heading: Force–extension curves and the spring balance
paragraphs: Typical graph: straight rise (proportional) → knee at limit of proportionality → yield point → necking → fracture. Every material that is ductile has necking; brittle materials snap without much stretch.
Spring balance measures force by stretching a spring and reading the scale — direct reading of newtons (or grams-force). For accurate work, calibrate with known masses (mg).
A spring bend beyond the elastic limit never returns; repeated loadings hysteresis loop — internal energy lost as heat over each cycle — used in automobile shock absorbers deliberately.
bullets: graph stages: straight → knee → yield → fracture
spring balance: stretch ∝ pull
hysteresis: energy loss by cycle, used in dampers
content.takeaway: The spring is just a stretchy ruler — read it honestly and it answers you back.

check.question: The gradient of a force vs extension graph gives
check.why: For F = kx, gradient = k.

content.heading: Work done in stretching a spring
paragraphs: Work done = Force × distance; but F = kx grows linearly, so the average force on the trip is ½kx; work = ½kx².
Equivalently, work done in stretching a spring = area under the F–extension graph (triangle or trapezium). JAMB loves that reading; the question says 'area under the graph' as an obfuscator for ½kx².
Work per unit volume: energy density in stretched material = ½ × stress × strain = ½ F x ÷ (A L). A stiffer spring stores more energy per volume; that's why bows are springy and trampolines work.
bullets: W = ½kx² for a linear spring
area under F–extension graph = stored energy
energy density = ½ stress × strain
content.takeaway: Half the spring’s force, full the spring’s X — that is the tiny-workman’s title deed.

check.question: The work done stretching a spring from zero to extension x is
check.why: F grows linearly with x, so work = average force × extension = ½kx × x = ½kx².

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: ½ is your friend: ½kx² for work, ½ stress × strain for density, ½ × base × height for F–x triangle. If the answer lacks ½, you skipped the average.

content.problem: A spring extends by 0.05 m when a 10 N force is applied. Find (a) its spring constant, (b) the work done extending it by that amount.

steps.reason: F = kx — force and extension ride together. Best: Hooke’s law directly. If energy is also asked, use W = ½kx².
steps.predictPrompt: At 5 N, how much would the same spring stretch?

steps.reason: W = ½kx² (equivalently ½Fx)
steps.predictPrompt: A second way to compute it — which one did you trust more?

content.question: A wire 3 m long, cross-section 2 × 10⁻⁶ m², stretches 0.01 m under a 1000 N load. Find Young’s modulus.

content.heading: A harder worked example: energy stored in a stretched wire
content.problem: A copper wire of natural length 2 m and Young’s modulus 1.2 × 10¹¹ N/m² is stretched by 80 mm using a load. Cross-sectional area 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². Find (a) the load, (b) the energy stored.

steps.reason: Young’s modulus is a ratio of stress to strain. Best: Y = (F/A) ÷ (ΔL/L). If energy comes next, use W = ½FΔL.
steps.predictPrompt: Units: does ΔL need to be in metres here?

steps.reason: W = ½ F · ΔL
steps.predictPrompt: Would W = ½kΔL² also work — if so, what is k?

content.heading: Go deeper: force–extension graphs in exam dress
paragraphs: Graph anatomy: straight line from origin rises hooke-ly; it kinks at the limit of proportionality, bends down past the elastic limit (permanent set), yields with increasing strain under barely more stress, then necks and snaps.

Diagnostic read: the knee is the last moment where Hooke applies; the yield point is where bonds snap in earnest; the breaking point is fracture; a material's twilight records stress relaxing amid growing strain without extra force.
JAMB's numbers live in gigapascals — anywhere near '5 × 10¹⁰ Pa' is metal under test; '5 × 10⁹' is polymer; hair at '5 × 10⁷' is everyday fibre; the magnitudes separate metals from rope.

In JAMB the last line of hope: 'gradient gives' — answer: spring constant (k). 'Which material is stiffest from the curves' — steepest graph wins. 'Which is strongest' — the one yielding at the highest force.

The point where a material fractures is the breaking point; between proportional limit and fracture is plastic range: only breaking the shape, not Hooke — but the body refuses to recover when the load releases.
bullets: straight line stops at limit of proportionality
yield point → necking → fracture
steepest gradient = stiffest = largest k
content.takeaway: Read the graph like a doctor reads an ECG — steep lines speak loudest.

content.heading: Go deeper: Young’s modulus across the material world
paragraphs: Units of Y: N/m² (or Pa). Y for steel ~2 × 10¹¹; copper ~1.1 × 10¹¹; aluminium ~0.7 × 10¹¹; brass ~1 × 10¹¹; rubber ~10⁷ — seven orders of magnitude. JAMB loves a comparison like 'a copper and steel wire stretched the same, which springs back less'.
Wire stretched under load: δl = FL/(AY). Both sides and A have same stretch difference — double length doubles extension, double A halves it; Y multiplies inverse for craft formulas.

Elastic potential energy stored in a wire: U = ½ Y A Δl² ÷ L = ½ F² L/(Y A). This is the reason elasticity drains in a rubber band looped around a tree trunk — pull/release thousands of times and the material grows warm: internal friction at molecular bonds dissolves stored energy.
bullets: δl = FL ÷ (A Y)
stiffer → less stretch; higher ΔY = harder
elastic energy = ½ F Δl = ½ Y A Δl² ÷ L
content.takeaway: Young’s modulus is the springboard rate — jumps stiffer = shorter trampoline.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets elasticity questions
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'load-extension graph', gradient = k; (2) 'find Young's modulus from F, x, L, A' — one target formula rearrangement; (3) 'two materials compared' — Y with bigger number returns less stretch under the same load; (4) 'spring is stretched from x₁ to x₂ — work done' — ½k(x₂² − x₁²); (5) 'work done by F against spring' — area interpretation: piecewise trapezia; (6) 'spring balance reading in a lift' — apparent weight, a.

Backup rule: the difference trick saves the day every time — work = ½k x₂² − ½k x₁²; the same formula reads as the area of the strip underneath the F–x curve; both views are true and the exam loves to mix them.

Trap: 'if the load doubles, the extension halves' — wrong: Hooke directs × 2; trap: 'the work done stretching is ½ F x' — true; trap: 'beyond proportional limit hooke remains' — wrong: beyond that everything is plastic.

Once more to wheels: measuring stiffness of metal plate 'a plate bent 2 mm under a load of 500 N' — if the problem wants Y, cross-section geometry is given; if extension falls beyond elastic limit, Y no longer applies — JAMB reminds you rather than tricks.
bullets: gradient = k; Δl formula = FL/(AY)
½k(x₂² − x₁²) when stretch grows from x₁ to x₂
beyond elastic limit — no Hooke
content.takeaway: Hooke manages the light loads; beyond limit, new rules apply.

lessons.title: Pressure and the Atmosphere
lessons.objective: State the SI unit of pressure, name and use pressure-measuring instruments (mercury barometer, aneroid barometer, manometer); relate variation of pressure with height; use a barometer as an altimeter.

content.heading: Pressure and the Atmosphere
paragraphs: Press a fingertip into the table — the indentation is pressure at work. A tyre pump presses air into a space tiny enough to hold it. Atmospheric pressure is the heavier air pressing on your whole body with every breath.

content.heading: Pressure, units and measurement
paragraphs: Pressure is force per unit area: P = F ÷ A. Unit: pascal (Pa) = N/m². Atmospheric pressure at sea level ≈ 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa = 101 kPa = 76 cm Hg = 760 mm Hg.

Measurement instruments: mercury barometer — long glass tube filled with mercury, open end down in a dish; clear column ≈ 76 cm — measures atmospheric pressure directly; aneroid barometer — flexible metal box, needle reads pressure, used in weather-cocks; manometer — U-tube, difference of heights inside and outside is pressure difference.
Useful conversions: 1 cm Hg ≈ 1333 Pa; 1 mm Hg = 1 torr ≈ 133 Pa; 1 atmosphere = 760 mm Hg = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa.
bullets: 1 Pa = 1 N/m²
1 atm ≈ 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 760 mm Hg
mercury barometer, aneroid barometer, manometer — the three instruments
content.takeaway: Pressure is the tide of the air — always pressing, always winning.

check.question: The SI unit of pressure is
check.why: P = F ÷ A — the pascal is N/m².

content.heading: Variation of pressure with height
paragraphs: Pressure falls with height — 90% of air sits below 10 km; Everest's summit holds < 30% of sea-level pressure.

A barometer reads the weight of the air column pressing on top. As you climb the column above you shortens; pressure falls. The rate of fall is approximately exponential — atmospheric pressure at 30 km is about 1% of sea level.
Altimeter: a sensitive aneroid barometer labelled in metres — an aircraft reads altitude by the pressure drop. The principle is the same one you use to guess your altitude at Lagos's altitude.
bullets: pressure falls off with height — air is compressible
altimeter = aneroid barometer calibrated in metres
10 km: ~26% of sea level; 30 km: ~1%
content.takeaway: The higher you look, the thinner the sea of air above.

check.question: As an aircraft climbs, the reading on an aneroid altimeter
options: rises — altimeter reads higher numbers at altitude
check.why: Less atmospheric pressure above the plane — calibrated as greater height.

content.heading: The mercury barometer and the altimeter
paragraphs: Mercury barometer anatomy: a glass tube about 1 m long, closed at one end, filled with mercury and inverted into a dish of mercury; vacuum space forms at the top; the column height equals atmospheric pressure — 760 mm at sea level, lower with rain, higher before rain falls.

Porbarometer; aneroid; manometer — differences: aneroid measures atmospheric pressure relative flexibility (weather), manometer measures pressure difference between a tank and outside or between two points, often for gas or vacuum systems.
Altimeter: pressure drops roughly 10% per kilometre. That is all JAMB wants from you.
bullets: mercury barometer: vacuum on top, 76 cm Hg at sea level
aneroid: no liquid — used for planes and weather
manometer: U-tube compares two pressures
content.takeaway: Three instruments, one job: pin down the push of the air.

check.question: A mercury barometer reads 76 cm at sea level. At a mountain top, the reading would typically be
check.why: Less air above the mountain, so the column supported is smaller.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Trio: 76 cm Hg = 760 mm Hg ≈ 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa; falling barometer = rain coming.

content.problem: A barometer reads 74 cm. Convert this to N/m². (g = 10; mercury ρ = 13600 kg/m³)

steps.reason: P = ρgh — directly from the fluid column. Best: density × gravity × height — no area needed. If only area is printed, use P = F ÷ A.
steps.predictPrompt: Give me the column height in metres before the formula.

steps.reason: P = ρgh. Best: depth sets pressure, not the shape. If the question asks, add the atmosphere to get P = ρgh + P_atm.
steps.predictPrompt: Which gives a familiar number — would you say 100,640 or more likely 101,000?

content.question: A man climbs a hill. His barometer readings drop from 76 cm to 70 cm. Estimate his height above sea level. Take g = 10 m/s², ρₐᵢᵣ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³.
hints: ΔP = ρₘₑᵣᶜᵤʳʸ g Δh — pressure-per-unit-length cancels with ρ air
ΔP = (0.76 − 0.70) × 13,600 × 10 = 8,160 Pa — pressure difference in Pascals

content.heading: A harder worked example: siphon and pressure difference
content.problem: A manometer reads 15 cm against atmosphere. Find the gas pressure in Pa. (mercury ρ = 13600 kg/m³, g = 10)

steps.reason: the pressure difference from the mercury column. Best: ρgh on the difference only. If asked total, P = 1 atm ± ρgh.
steps.predictPrompt: 0.15 m is 15 cm — watch the units.

steps.reason: gas could be at higher or lower pressure than air — we need the context
steps.result: if the gas is above 1 atm → 101,325 + 20,400 = 121,725 Pa; if below → 80,925 Pa
steps.predictPrompt: Is 'higher' or 'lower' the likely context for a manometer?

content.heading: Go deeper: barometer mechanics
paragraphs: Mercury column hangs suspended by air's push; remove the air pressure and the vacuum holds the column suspended 760 mm tall by its own weight. Water is about 13.6 times less dense than mercury, so a water barometer would need a column of ≈ 10.3 m — Torricelli proved that it's not the tube's material holding it; it's the weight of the air above.

Barometer waves: pressure falls before rain arrives; pressure rises during dry seasons; storm forecasts once depended entirely on mercury barometers. Wind is the sucking, the vacuum pulls it before any droplet forms.

Aneroid vs mercury: aneroid is mechanical — a sealed thin box, a spring, a link to a pointer; simpler to read at extreme altitude; almost universally used in aircraft. Mercury is more precise — lab work.
bullets: Torricelli's invention: 1643 — the weight of the air itself, proven
water column of 10.3 m — one atmosphere can hold it
aneroid for portable height; mercury for precision labs
content.takeaway: A 76 cm column of mercury = same press as air: balance at the top.

content.heading: Go deeper: pressure above and below sea level
paragraphs: Pressure halves about every 5.5 km: sea level ≈ 101 kPa, 5.5 km ≈ 50 kPa, 11 km ≈ 25 kPa. Underwater, pressure rises by ≈ 1 atm every 10 m — 20 m depth feels like 3 atm total.
Aircraft cabins pressurise to ~1 atm because tissue would fail without; mountain climbers risk altitude sickness above 3 km where pressure is ~70% of sea level.
At sea level the air overhead is about 100,000 pascals; at 5 km only a third; at Mount Everest summit (8.8 km) atmosphere sits at about 30%. Climbers breathe oxygen bottles and acclimatise for days.
Diving at depth accepts the same 1 atm per 10 m of seawater — 20 m deep sees 3 atmospheres; anything shallower than 30 m is recreational-safe territory in exam tradition.
Weather pressure numbers: 1012 hPa is normal; 1000 hPa falling = rain coming; 1025 hPa rising = fair. JAMB never asks real-time numbers — textbook numbers instead.
bullets: diving: +1 atm per 10 m depth
altitude sickness > 3 km
1013 hPa sea level; falls with altitude — check instrument
content.takeaway: Pressure writes itself from stratosphere to sea floor.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets atmospheric-pressure questions
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'a column of mercury sits at 76 cm' — straight P = ρgh; (2) 'the barometer is taken to a mountain' — new reading, compare; (3) 'find the depth in water equivalent to 76 cm Hg' — ρₘgh matches ρ_w h_w; (4) 'aneroid vs mercury' — purpose comparison; (5) 'air pressure at sea level' — 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa / 760 mm Hg; (6) 'flight altitude read from pressure' — 10% drops per kilometre approximate.

Traps: 'the column in the mercury barometer has vacuum, but the air presses nowhere' — wrong: completely opposite — vacuum exerts no pressure, so it absorbs the column's own weight by falling; trap: 'water columns work equally' — yes, but the column would stand 10.3 m; trap: 'mass of air above your head' — roughly 10 tonnes per square metre — overwhelming intuition reset.
Conversion between mmHg and Pascals — 1 mmHg = 133 Pa; JAMB never reverses, always forward; remember 13.6 × ρ water and you're safe.
The whole toolkit: 1 cm Hg = 133 Pa; 1 atm ≈ 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa; 10.3 m water column holds the same weight of air — learn the trio cold.
bullets: P = ρgh — the only formula needed today
10.34 m equivalent water column
aneroid vs mercury: clarity vs. sensitivity
content.takeaway: Three dozen conversions, one equals sign armed on every page.

lessons.title: Pressure in Liquids
lessons.objective: Relate pressure to depth and density (P = ρgh); apply Pascal’s principle of transmission of pressure; solve hydraulic problems; explain applications in brakes and car lifts.

content.heading: Pressure in Liquids
paragraphs: Press on a deep pond; water presses back far harder. Swim one metre down — your ears do the rest of the talking. Liquids carry the push of gravity directly on every cubic centimetre of their volume.

content.heading: Pressure, depth and density
paragraphs: P = ρgh: pressure at a depth h below the surface of a liquid of density ρ. Specific cases require g = 9.8 or 10 m/s²; ρ for water = 1000 kg/m³.

The pressure at all points at the same level in one static liquid is identical. It does not depend on the shape of the vessel — a pool, a swimming tunnel, a U-tube bent the same depth still read the same.
Total pressure at a depth h in a liquid open to the atmosphere = atmosphere + ρgh. In sealed tanks, only liquid head remains.
bullets: P = ρgh — at every point on a level
shape independent for static liquids
open tank: add 1 atm on top of ρgh
content.takeaway: The uniform rule: depth decides, head follows.

check.question: Pressure in a static liquid depends on the
check.why: ρgh — only depth and density, never shape.

content.heading: Pascal’s principle and hydraulic machines
paragraphs: Pascal’s principle: pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted undiminished in all directions. In a tube open at both ends, a small force on a small piston raises the pressure in the whole tube — and a large piston at one end responds with a big force.

Hydraulic vehicle lift: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ — small effort pushes large mass up with essentially the same pressure everywhere. You sit in the driver's seat and press the foot-brake — brake fluid transmits the force to all four wheels instantly.
Hydraulic brake lines leak easily — air bubble ruins pressure transfer, hence bleeding. Car jacks, forklift rams, aircraft flap actuators — all Pascal.
bullets: ρgh rules once at the surface; P = F/A for applied force elsewhere
F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ for hydraulic: pressure is the same

content.heading: Go deeper: honest numbers in liquids
paragraphs: Lake pressure on a diver: pressure increases by ~10,000 Pa per metre — an extra atmosphere per 10 m. In Lagos Bay on a calm day, every villager knows the swimming rule: deeper = things heavier on the eardrums.

Wording matters — gauge pressure starts at zero; absolute pressure starts from vacuum. When the question says 'due to the water column' it wants the bare ρgh; when it says 'total pressure' it wants the sum with atmosphere.

Brake systems: a tiny hole means vapour/pressure failure; double cylinder requires identical pressure at all wheels; modern electronic programs do brake balance internally. Bicycle quirks share the same principle — a bleed loop banishes air and the pedal returns to honesty.

You stop the nightmare: a sealed hydraulic line behaves uniformly; open-top overflow tanks beat Pascal; trick questions will pit 'total pressure' against 'the due-to-water pressure' — read the wording and keep both numbers ready.
Bench-top estimate for any pool: 1 m of water adds ~10,000 Pa — twice at 2 m depth-total-head; tanks and swimming pools both pay with walls at the deep end.
One height-order check: adult human breathing at 2 m below surface feels twice standard water-push — depth is always a small linear debt against ρgh.

content.heading: Go deeper: Pascal’s principle in every system domestic
paragraphs: Pascal lived at a time of cart wheels and taverns; his law works just the same today: press a small area with F small; the same pressure reaches every point of the fluid. This is the hydraulic jack, the car brake, the forklift, the aircraft landing gear — everything we trust.

Transmission fluid isn't magic: it's the same density anywhere, incompressible enough to treat as rigid body for steady-state motion. The pressure is high but so is the leverage: F₂ = F₁ × A₂/A₁ — Pascal's trick for making small efforts move tons.
And the system breaks if air gets in — air compresses, liquids do not; bicycle brakes develop the same failure the same way.

content.takeaway: A sealed fluid is a secret handshake — pressure switched before anyone says a word.

lessons.title: Liquids at Rest: Density, Archimedes and Floatation
lessons.objective: Determine densities of solids and liquids (measuring cylinder, density bottle); define relative density; find upthrust on a body immersed; apply Archimedes’ principle and the law of floatation (ships, hydrometers).

content.heading: Liquids at Rest
paragraphs: Float a piece of cork on water — it bobs back up. So does a ship; so does an airship. Archimedes proved 2,200 years back why: a body immersed in fluid pushes fluid away — and that displaced fluid pushes back.

content.heading: Density: measured and compared
paragraphs: Density of a solid: mass ÷ volume. Solids: measure volume by displacement (overflow can or measuring cylinder). Liquids: weigh empty beaker, weigh with liquid, weigh with water — compare.
Relative density (specific gravity) of a substance = its density ÷ density of water. No units — it's a ratio. Relative density of mercury = 13.6; steel 7.8; aluminium 2.7.
Density bottle: measure mass empty, with water, with the test liquid — same volume; simple subtraction and division gives relative density of the liquid accurately.

content.takeaway: Density is mass per space — relative density is a comparison with water.

content.heading: Upthrust on immersed bodies
paragraphs: Every body in a fluid receives an upward push — upthrust. Its magnitude equals the weight of the displaced fluid. A denser block of iron sinks because its displaced fluid weighs less; wood floats because it displaces its own weight of water.
For a totally immersed body: upthrust = weight of fluid with volume equal to the body's volume. For a partly immersed floating body: upthrust = the body's own weight.
U-tube terms: if the upthrust from displaced water is 20 N, the body 'loses' 20 N in water — spring balance reads less; in air it reads its true weight.

content.takeaway: Upthrust pays you back whatever you displace — water wants you out.

content.heading: Archimedes’ principle and floatation
paragraphs: Archimedes’ principle: a body fully or partly immersed in a fluid displaces an equal weight of that fluid — upthrust equals that weight. Mathematically U = ρVg (for uniform bodies).

Law of floatation: a floating body displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight; it takes the position where its centre of buoyancy and its centre of gravity stay on the same vertical line. Stability: wide hull, low centre → stable (ship at sea).

Applications: ships — massive but hull spreads weight; submarines — ballast tanks control depth; hydrometer — weighted bulb floats higher in denser liquids; laundromats use hydrometers to assess alcohol syrup; fuel gauges in cars are simple hydrometers.

content.heading: Go deeper: overflow measurement and density bottles
paragraphs: Overflow can: fill to brim; drop a body in; water spills out into a collecting cylinder — volume of displaced water = volume of body. Use for irregular solids. For a sinker: volume = weight out / (ρg) — or simply measure the displaced water volume.
Density bottle: typical 25 cm³ calibration; fill with water; dry and weigh; refill with test liquid; dry and weigh; subtract. Hitting 100 g accurately for water is the key — subtract the tare.

content.heading: Go deeper: ships, submarines and hydrometers
paragraphs: Ships: a 10,000-ton ship floats because its average density (steel + air) is less than water; the hollowing steel hull displaces volume equal to its total weight. The waterline versus load marks — known as Plimsoll lines — tell harbour officers exactly how much stays above.
Seawater is about 3% denser than fresh water (1025 vs 1000 kg/m³), so the same ship sits higher afloat at sea and lower inland — a niche detail JAMB loves to slip into flotation stems.
Submarine: pump ballast tanks with water to sink; blow with compressed air to surface; depth control by minute adjustments — the same submerged/undisturbed bargain the whale and the piton fish keep.

Hydrometer: graduated glass tube with lead shot, floating higher in denser fluid; used for battery acid, milk, alcohol and fuels; car battery density runs ~1.1 (flat) to ~1.2 (full). JAMB also trades in 'relative density' stems — float/sink the same substance in two liquids.

content.heading: Go deeper: how JAMB sets liquids-at-rest questions
paragraphs: Archetypes: (1) 'a floating body displaces X ml of water — weight?' — equals weight of displaced fluid; (2) 'relative density from bottle readings' — three masses; (3) 'will solid of density Y float in water' — check number vs 1000; (4) 'two immiscible liquids mix in a flask — what's on top?' — lighter first (oil on water); (5) 'upthrust on fully immersed' — ρgV; (6) 'a fish and a stone — which sinks?' — density beats; (7) 'if a body displaces more than its own mass of water, it floats' — always own-weight displaced at equilibrium.

Traps: 'relative density matters' — never with unit; '0.8 sinks in water' — no, floats; 'displacement counts only when immersed' — yes; 'a cork weighs less than 1 newton will float' — check before you leap; 'heavier than displaced liquid fails' — correct framing, not a shortcut; 'a swimmer floats by lungs full of air' — density decreases, upthrust same, rise.

Remember: ρgV always; answer in newtons or grams times g. If you see 'remaining fraction submerged' — use ratio of densities; if you see 'float related to specific gravity' — no unit; if asked for 'what weight must be added to make it sink' — subtract displaced vs body weight.
